item.title: Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit
item.dc:creator: Alex Lavaee, Matthai Philipose
item.description:
AI agents can generate code at a scale that’s hard for humans to review line-by-line. PDD Kit helps ensure the code is doing what the developer intended by creating formal specifications and testing against them. It converts developer intent into a Verus specification, proves AI-generated code meets it for every input, and uses tests where proofs aren't practical. Developers review intent, not every line.

The post Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit appeared first on Microsoft Research.
item.content:encoded:
At a glance

  • Formal methods for everyday software. PDD Kit helps you turn your intent into a formal spec, then proves the code your agent writes for every input and uses tests where a proof can’t reach. It takes formal methods beyond niche, specialist work to engineers without a formal methods background and to everyday applications, like the full-stack web app shown here.
  • Exhaustive line-by-line human review can become difficult to scale as AI agents generate increasingly large amounts of code. The plan is supposed to be the contract between you and a coding agent, but nothing actually forces the agent to follow it. The tests it writes usually check what it built, rather than what you asked for. 
  • PDD Kit makes the agent keep the plan. It works with you to turn your intent into a formal specification in Verus (opens in new tab), proves the agent’s code meets that spec for every input, and falls back to tests where a proof can’t reach.
  • We tried it on a full-stack web app. Inside GitHub Next’s Chopin (opens in new tab), we used PDD Kit to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust (opens in new tab) storefront. Verus hardened the code and uncovered existing bugs, proving the absence of login bugs with respect to the specification. The developer reviewed the intent and never read the generated code line-by-line. 

The plan is the contract the agent should follow, but nothing constrains the agent to follow it.

Coding agents now ship whole features in one sitting often spanning tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of lines of code. As a result, reading every line of the pull request doesn’t scale to this new way of work. Now, most teams invest in the plan and relevant testing instead: describe to an agent what they want, go back and forth until the plan and proposed tests look right, and hand them off to the agent for implementation. 

This plan or natural language spec is meant to be the contract that an agent holds. However, in practice, the agent can drift from it. It implements something slightly different, then writes tests that pass for its implementation rather than the code you intended it to write. Continuous integration (CI) grows due to a profusion of low quality and high quantity of tests, coverage looks healthy, and the gap between what you asked for and what shipped stays hidden until a bug report or a nasty edge case shows up.

So, how do you reliably scale review as agents generate increasingly large amounts of code? Agent code fails in two ways a careful reviewer would usually catch: it leaves out something obviously necessary, or it does something obviously wrong. Tests alone don’t close that gap, because they only exercise a tiny slice of what a program can do. Closing it needs a different kind of machinery, which is where proofs come in.

Review asks “does this look right?” A proof answers “is this right?” A mathematical proof shows that code meets its specification for every input, including the ones your test suite can miss. That provides stronger assurance for specified properties than testing alone, especially when line-by-line review isn’t practical.

Proofs used to be too expensive for everyday software. You needed specialists, unfamiliar languages, proofs many times larger than the code, and proofs took years to develop, but two things have changed since. First, recent advances in coding agents have made it increasingly practical for them to help generate formal proofs from well-defined specs. Secondly, agents can now better help you write formal specs. We call this new software development paradigm Proof-Driven Development (PDD). PDD Kit is our toolkit for it.

How PDD Kit works

PDD Kit is to formal methods roughly what Spec Kit (opens in new tab) is to Spec-Driven Development. It runs as a partner inside Chopin (opens in new tab), GitHub Next’s real-time, multiplayer planning environment, where a team and agents can plan in one shared document.

The workflow has two halves (Figure 1). First, team members review intent in plain language. PDD Kit asks the questions a careful reviewer would ask, explains the relevant code as it goes, and records the answers in an intent artifact, a document that bridges the user’s intent with the formal specification or tests. The parts of the user’s intent that can be formalized are converted into formal specifications and the rest, which must be taken on trust, are converted to informal specifications for tests. PDD Kit automatically generates proofs that the code satisfies the derived formal specs and high-quality tests for the informal specs. You don’t need a formal methods background for any of it. 

Consequently, every result in PDD Kit says which kind of verification it rests on: 

  • Formal verification is a mathematical proof that code satisfies its specification for every possible input, checked by a tool called a verifier. For PDD Kit today, that verifier is Verus (opens in new tab), a proof language for Rust co-developed by Microsoft Research, Carnegie Mellon University, VMware Research, ETH Zurich, MPI-SWS, UNSW Sydney, the University of Texas at Austin, the University of Michigan, the University of British Columbia, the University of Wisconsin–Madison and the Weizmann Institute of Science.
  • Empirical verification checks code by running it and observing what it does. It covers what a proof can’t reach, such as a third-party cryptography library or a user interface. It uses unit and end-to-end tests, terminal automation, browser agents, and computer-use agents for anything a browser can’t drive. A passing test only shows the code worked on the inputs it tried, so PDD Kit labels it as evidence rather than proof.

The line between the two is the Trusted Computing Base (TCB): the code that the proof assumes behaves as described. PDD Kit makes that line explicit and asks you to sign off on each piece. 

The capstone: a full-stack web app

To show PDD Kit integrating with existing codebases, we built Pet Store, a full-stack web app written entirely in Rust (opens in new tab). The backend uses Axum (opens in new tab) and SQLite (opens in new tab) and handles inventory, promotions, orders and checkout. The storefront is a Leptos (opens in new tab) app compiled to WebAssembly (opens in new tab). Together they come to about 5,000 lines of Rust.

For brevity in this blog, we focus on formally verifying the login logic of the app, but the same process can be used to verify functional correctness of the entire app. PDD Kit recommends starting with the most sensitive parts of your application and incrementally verifying your application. A login bug can hand an attacker a customer’s account or an admin’s controls, so that’s where proof effort pays off first. The developer’s whole request in Chopin was two sentences: 

Verify the login logic in backend/src/handlers/auth.rs. Here are my requirements:

  1. You only get a token with the right password.
  2. Only admin accounts get admin tokens.

We kept the request rough on purpose. Capturing the intent of the user and turning the user request into something a proof can check is PDD Kit’s job.

Step 1: Questions before code

PDD Kit’s planning workflow, pdd-plan, reads the code and comes back, before writing anything, with questions in a Decisions tab. When a question depends on how the code works, the card explains that part first: the goal, how the pieces fit, and the exact function involved, so you can answer without opening the source. 

The question looks pedantic, but it matters. “You only get a token with the right password” rules out the bad case, a wrong password getting a token, and a login that refuses everyone keeps that promise perfectly. “The right password always works” is the half that rules it out. Formally, the first is an implication (token ⇒ right password) and the second is its converse. Together they make an “if and only if.” An agent left alone would pick one without telling you, but here the developer picked both ways.

Step 2: A human readable intent map

As the conversation goes on, PDD Kit keeps a rough work section at the top of the plan current, so a user can keep track of important concepts without having to scroll back through a long chat to find what was agreed. It includes a flowchart of the login being specified, a spec landscape of what will be proved and what will be trusted, and, when a picture helps, a mental model. For login, PDD Kit drew a ticket desk (Figure 3).

Below it, the intent map ties each requirement back to the developer’s own words and records how it was settled (Figure 4). Each entry links to the section of the formal spec that models it and to the tests that cover it, and the spec section shows snippets of the Verus contract, annotated so the developer can see how the formal spec models their intent.

The decision card in Figure 2 is the kind of ambiguity an agent would otherwise settle silently. Figure 5 shows how small the difference looks on paper: the two readings disagree in a single cell, a right password that gets no token.

Step 3: Proving the login function

Before anything gets built, PDD Kit asks the team to sign off on the plan as a whole. Its first draft proved the decision at the center of login, picking the table and gating on the password, and kept the handler around it trusted and tested. That’s a sensible default, and it’s what PDD Kit recommended, but the developer wanted more. The handler is where the lookups get awaited and the token gets signed, and that glue is exactly where a refactor can quietly swap two lines. So at intent review the developer chose to give the login handler its own async spec, so the proof covers that glue too instead of trusting it (Figure 6).

That choice moved almost everything into the proof and left the login handler with nothing to do but unpack the request. A new async function, login_flow, carries the contract from the request’s fields all the way to the token or the HTTP error. PDD Kit then brought the revised plan back for a fresh sign-off, because matching your intent isn’t proof, and it doesn’t approve new trust or a wider scope. 

Step 4: Where proof stops

There are plenty of things you can’t prove about a program, and login runs into most of them:

  • Code the verifier can’t see. bcrypt’s hashing, sqlx’s queries and jsonwebtoken’s signing live in other crates, outside the proof. 
  • Facts about the outside world. What SQLite holds right now and what time the clock says are inputs to the program, not something its code can establish. 
  • Whether, and how fast, something finishes. The spec says what you get if login answers. A hung query, or a slow one, breaks nothing in it. 
  • Anything a person has to judge, like whether an error message helps or a screen makes sense. 
  • Whatever nobody wrote down. A proof covers its spec and says nothing about requirements outside it. 

That’s where empirical verification comes in. PDD Kit spells out the trusted boundary, the part of the TCB this proof leans on. It wraps each trusted piece in a small function with an assumed contract, using Verus’s #[verifier::external_body] or external_fn_specification, asks the developer to accept each one on its own, and writes a test for every assumed clause into the plan. For login, the developer signed off on six pieces:

  • The two lookups, Customer::find_by_email and Admin::find_by_username. Each awaited, successful lookup returns exactly the row its own table holds for that email or username, or none. 
  • check_password, a thin wrapper around bcrypt::verify. It errors only on a stored hash bcrypt can’t read, and Ok(true) means exactly the right password. 
  • generate_token, which signs exactly the claims it is given under the configured secret and reports a signing failure as a 500. 
  • expiry_from_now, which reads the clock and writes an expiry exactly 24 hours later. 
  • database_error, which turns a failed lookup into today’s 500 with sqlx’s message. 
  • The login handler shell, which unpacks the request and passes its fields to login_flow unchanged. 

In the spec, a lookup keeps its code where it is and gets a contract from the outside with external_fn_specification: 

/// Looks up a customer by exact email. 
/// Trusted, not proved: the SQL query runs in sqlx, which Verus cannot check. 
/// Every customer promise of `login_flow` rests on it. 
#[verifier::external_fn_specification] 
pub async fn ex_customer_find_by_email(pool: &sqlx::SqlitePool, email: &str) 
    -> (r: Result, sqlx::Error>) 
    ensures 
        // When the query succeeds, it returns the customers row on 
        // file for exactly this email, or None when there is none. 
        r matches Ok(found) ==> found == customer_on_file(email@), 
{ 
    Customer::find_by_email(pool, email).await 
} 

The clock is a small wrapper marked #[verifier::external_body]. Verus uses its ensures clause and never reads the body: 

/// Reads the clock and computes a token's expiry 24 hours ahead. 
/// Trusted, not proved: chrono's clock is outside the proof. 
/// It panics if the time is out of range, as today's login does; 
/// that panic is not promised against. 
#[verifier::external_body] 
pub fn expiry_from_now() -> (r: Expiry) 
    ensures 
        // The expiry is exactly 24 hours (86,400 seconds) after the clock reading. 
        r.exp as int == r.now as int + 86_400, 
{ 
    ... 
} 

Figure 7 puts the three layers together: what Verus proves, what people accept and tests check, and what nobody is promising. 

Figure 8 maps what gets proved and what gets trusted. Each trust decision is its own card. It shows the clauses Verus will take on faith, what the developer is accepting, and which promise falls apart if the assumption is wrong (Figure 9). Every assumed clause then gets an empirical check in the plan’s Empirical verification section, written as Given/When/Then scenarios before any test exists (Figure 10). An entry says planned until it has run, and then it records the command’s result and the commit it ran against.

The plan is just as explicit about what nobody is promising: that the login future ever completes, that an out-of-range clock won’t panic, anything about the timing or rate of attempts, and how other endpoints read the role. 

Step 5: Reading the spec

The intent artifact is what the team reviews. It’s the plain-language version of the formal spec PDD Kit writes as Verus contracts. You might be wondering whether someone now has to read the proof instead of the code. Nobody does, because the coding agent writes the proof and Verus checks every step of it. If Verus accepts the proof, it holds whether or not anyone reads it. The spec is what the proof is held to, so that’s what people review, and this one is short enough to learn to read in a few minutes. Each function gets an ensures block: statements about its result, r, that must hold for every possible input. Verus checks them when you build, and if any clause could fail for even one input, the build fails and Verus points at that clause. Each clause reads as an if-then, and Figure 11 takes apart the clause for the developer’s first requirement.

Notice that the same a appears on every line, which ties the password check to the token. For example, imagine a bug where login checks the password against one account but signs the token for another. Bob logs in with his own, correct password and gets back a token for Alice’s account. Each step looks fine on its own, but this clause catches it, because the password check and the token have to name the same account. That’s the kind of wiring bug a test suite rarely thinks to look for. The spec also has to talk about SQLite, bcrypt and JWTs without running any of them. It does that with uninterpreted functions, names with no body: customer_on_file(email) and admin_on_file(username) for the rows the database holds, bcrypt_verdict(password, hash) for what bcrypt would say, and token_claims(token, secret) for what a token carries. Verus knows nothing about them except what the trusted contracts from Step 4 promise. The proof says “whatever the database holds, login does the right thing with it,” and a trusted contract says “the lookup returns what the database holds.” 

/// The customers row the database holds for 
/// exactly this email, if any, when login looks. 
/// Left abstract: only `Customer::find_by_email`'s 
/// trusted contract says what it is. 
pub uninterp spec fn customer_on_file(email: Seq) -> Option; 
... 
/// What bcrypt says about `password` against a 
/// stored `hash`: Some(true) when it is the password 
/// the hash was made from, Some(false) when it is 
/// not, None when bcrypt cannot read the hash. 
/// Left abstract: its meaning is bcrypt's, taken on trust through `check_password`. 
pub uninterp spec fn bcrypt_verdict(password: Seq, hash: Seq) 
    -> Option; 
 
/// The password is the right one for the stored hash, by bcrypt's verdict. 
pub open spec fn password_matches(password: Seq, hash: Seq) -> bool { 
    bcrypt_verdict(password, hash) == Some(true) 
} 

On top of those, named_account(email, username) says which account a login names: the customers row for the email when one is sent, otherwise the admins row for the username, otherwise none. It’s written like Rust, but it’s a mathematical definition that never runs and only appears in contracts. Code like this is called ghost code, since the verifier checks it but the compiler erases it from the program. With it, the developer’s two-sentence request ends up as eight ensures clauses on login_flow (Figure 12). 

/// The account a login names: the customers row for 
/// the email when one is sent (role "customer"), 
/// otherwise the admins row for the username (role "admin"), otherwise none. 
pub open spec fn named_account(email: Option, username: Option) 
    -> Option { 
    match email { 
        Some(e) => match customer_on_file(e@) { 
            Some(c) => Some(NamedAccount { 
                id: c.id@, password_hash: c.password_hash@, role: customer_role() }), 
            None => None, 
        }, 
        None => match username { 
            Some(u) => match admin_on_file(u@) { 
                Some(a) => Some(NamedAccount { 
                    id: a.id@, password_hash: a.password_hash@, role: admin_role() }), 
                None => None, 
            }, 
            None => None, 
        }, 
    } 
} 

Here’s the whole contract, with its doc comment trimmed. Each clause has the plain-English comment above it that the intent artifact shows the team: 

/// The whole login, awaited end to end: from the 
/// request's fields to the token or the HTTP error. 
/// ... 
pub async fn login_flow(pool: &sqlx::SqlitePool, config: &Config, 
    email: Option, username: Option, password: &str) 
    -> (r: Result) 
    ensures 
        // Neither an email nor a username: 400 with today's message. 
        email is None && username is None 
            ==> (r matches Err(AppError::BadRequest(m)) 
                && m@ == missing_identity_text()), 
        // A token only for the account the login names, with its right 
        // password; it carries that account's id and its table's role. 
        r matches Ok(t) ==> (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) 
            && password_matches(password@, a.password_hash) 
            && token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) 
            && c.sub@ == a.id && c.role@ == a.role), 
        // The right password for the named account always gets a 
        // token, unless a lookup or signing failure gives 500. 
        (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) 
            && password_matches(password@, a.password_hash)) 
            ==> (r is Ok || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), 
        // A login naming an account nobody holds gets 
        // 401, unless the lookup fails with 500. 
        ((email is Some || username is Some) && named_account(email, username) is None) 
            ==> (r matches Err(AppError::Unauthorized) 
                || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), 
        // A wrong password for an account whose hash bcrypt 
        // can read gets 401, unless the lookup fails with 500. 
        (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) 
            && bcrypt_verdict(password@, a.password_hash) == Some(false)) 
            ==> (r matches Err(AppError::Unauthorized) 
                || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), 
        // An account whose stored hash bcrypt cannot read gets 500 and no token. 
        (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) 
            && bcrypt_verdict(password@, a.password_hash) is None) 
            ==> r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_)), 
        // The admin role only for an admins row 
        // found by username, with no email sent. 
        (r matches Ok(t) && token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) 
            && c.role@ == admin_role()) 
            ==> (email is None && username matches Some(u) 
                && admin_on_file(u@) is Some), 
        // An email login's token always carries the customer role. 
        (r matches Ok(t) && email is Some) 
            ==> (token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) 
                && c.role@ == customer_role()), 
{ 
    unimplemented!() 
} 

The trusted boundary shows up in the code too. check_password is one of the functions whose body Verus doesn’t check. Its contract ties it to bcrypt_verdict, an uninterpreted model of bcrypt with no axioms:

/// Asks bcrypt whether `password` matches the stored `hash`. 
/// Trusted, not proved: Verus cannot check bcrypt's hashing, 
/// so this wrapper's contract is assumed. 
/// Every password promise of `login_flow` rests on it. 
#[verifier::external_body] 
pub fn check_password(password: &str, hash: &str) -> (r: Result) 
    ensures 
        // bcrypt answers (Ok) exactly when it can read the stored hash. 
        r is Ok <==> bcrypt_verdict(password@, hash@) is Some, 
        // Its answer is its verdict: true for the 
        // right password, false for any other. 
        r matches Ok(b) ==> bcrypt_verdict(password@, hash@) == Some(b), 
{ 
    bcrypt::verify(password, hash).map_err(|e| e.to_string()) 
} 

The doc comment above it says what rests on it: every password promise of login_flow. Every login ends in one of a handful of places, and only one of them has a token (Figure 13). The proof covers all of them at once. 

login_flow is async: it awaits a database query. Verus can put contracts on async functions, with one rule worth knowing (Figure 14). requires is checked when the call creates the future. ensures describes the value you get when you await it. Nothing promises the future finishes, so a hung query breaks no clause. 

The doc comment on login_flow says so in as many words: 

/// ... No promise the future completes. 
pub async fn login_flow(...) -> (r: Result) 

login_flow stays short because it’s built from smaller proved pieces. lookup_target picks the table. login_core awaits the lookup and calls decide_login, the password gate. issue_token signs the token, or maps a refusal to today’s HTTP error. Each piece has its own contract, and Verus proves login_flow using only those contracts, without re-reading their bodies. Change the body of decide_login and only decide_login gets proved again. 

Here’s the smallest piece, whole, and the start and end of the password gate: 

pub fn lookup_target(email: Option, username: Option) 
    -> (r: Result) 
    ensures 
        // An email, when sent, wins: customers are searched for exactly that email. 
        email matches Some(e) 
            ==> r == Ok::(LookupTarget::CustomerByEmail(e)), 
        // With no email, a username sends the search 
        // to admins for exactly that username. 
        email is None && username matches Some(u) 
            ==> r == Ok::(LookupTarget::AdminByUsername(u)), 
        // With neither, the login is refused for missing an identity. 
        email is None && username is None 
            ==> r == Err::(LoginError::MissingIdentity), 

pub fn decide_login(target: &LookupTarget, found: Option, password: &str) 
    -> (r: Result) 
    ensures 
        // No row found: refused as Unauthorized, 
        // the same answer as a wrong password. 
        found is None 
            ==> r == Err::(LoginError::Unauthorized), 
        // Claims come back only for a found row 
        // whose stored hash matches the password. 
        r is Ok ==> found is Some 
            && password_matches(password@, found->Some_0.password_hash@), 
        // The right password for a found row always gets claims. 
        found matches Some(a) && password_matches(password@, a.password_hash@) 
            ==> r is Ok, 
        ... 
        // An admins-table search gives the role text "admin". 
        r matches Ok(c) && target is AdminByUsername ==> c.role@ == admin_role(), 
        // A customers-table search gives the role text "customer". 
        r matches Ok(c) && target is CustomerByEmail ==> c.role@ == customer_role(), 

An overview of login.rs 

Figure 15 maps the whole spec file, verified/src/login.rs. It reads top to bottom in four layers: headers, imports and types Verus needs to know about, an abstract view of the outside world, the trusted contracts that connect that view to real code, and the five contracts the proof has to meet.  

Here are two of the less obvious parts, abridged. external_type_specification introduces a type Verus didn’t define. The pool stays opaque, while a customers row keeps its fields visible: 

/// The connection pool, opaque to the proof: only 
/// the lookups' contracts say what it returns. 
#[verifier::external_type_specification] 
#[verifier::external_body] 
#[verifier::reject_recursive_types(DB)] 
pub struct ExPool(sqlx::Pool); 
... 
/// A customers row, with its fields visible to the proof. 
#[verifier::external_type_specification] 
pub struct ExCustomer(Customer); 

And LoginError keeps the decision separate from the HTTP response, which is what lets issue_token pin each refusal to today’s status code: 

/// Why a login gets no token. 
pub enum LoginError { 
    /// Neither an email nor a username was sent: 400 Bad Request. 
    MissingIdentity, 
    /// No such account, or the password does not match: 401 Unauthorized. 
    Unauthorized, 
    /// bcrypt could not read the stored hash, with its message: 500 Internal. 
    UnreadableHash(String), 
    /// The lookup query failed: 500 Internal, with sqlx's message. 
    Database(sqlx::Error), 
} 

Before the plan comes back to you, two reviewer agents poke holes in the derived formal spec from the intent artifact to ensure a high-quality translation, so that the spec matches what you asked for and doesn’t promise more than a proof could show. The spec refinement runs in the background and takes live user feedback, iterating until reviewers agree that the spec is sound. 

Step 6: Prove, check, close the gaps 

Signing off on the spec is where the developer’s review ends. Everything after it, the implementation and the proof, is checked by machines, which is why this post spends its time on the spec and not the proof. Once the developer signs off, a Build plan stage (Figure 16) hands the approved plan to pdd-prove, which turns it into a small task graph (Figure 16). For login, that’s seven tasks: get login.rs building under Verus inside the backend crate, prove the decision, the token and the whole flow, then write the tests for the trusted wrappers and the end-to-end login. 

Each task runs the same loop: 

  • A coding agent writes the implementation and the proof, and Verus checks them against the derived formal spec. 
  • Anything in the trusted boundary gets the tests the plan called for. 
  • An LLM verifier reads the plan, the specification and the results side by side, and looks for gaps: requirements with no proof and no passing check. Gaps go back to the coding agent until none remain. If the specification itself has a gap, such as two requirements that contradict each other, it comes back to the developer as a decision. 

A proof is only as good as its spec, so pdd-prove checks the spec too. When a model writes its own spec, or is tuned to produce proofs, it tends to land on weak invariants: clauses that verify but rule out almost nothing. They prove something, just rarely the thing you care about. We call that “vibe verification.” That’s why it’s so important to make sure your intent is aligned with the agent and what PDD Kit is great for. 

The loop is strict about not moving the goalposts. If an async construct can’t be expressed in the pinned Verus, the task stops and asks the team instead of switching to a non-async helper or weakening a contract. 

How does PDD Kit remove classes of bugs? The mutation check is how PDD Kit guards against vibe verification. pdd-prove plants one bug per ensures clause in a scratch copy of the code, like refusing everyone or checking the username before the email, and Verus has to reject each mutant on the clause it targets. A mutant that gets through means that clause constrains nothing, and it comes back as a gap. 

Step 7: Review intent alongside verified code

When the tasks pass, pdd-prove opens pull requests. They add a verified/ crate with login_flow, its pieces, their proofs, and the trusted wrappers with their tests, and route the real login handler through login_flow, keeping the existing HTTP status codes. Your verified logic integrates with and hardens your production login path, not a copy of it. 

The developer was able to merge without relying on exhaustive line-by-line review of the generated code. The review had already happened on the intent artifact this whole time, where the team has the final say. We shifted more of the review focus from code review to intent review. The pull request works as a receipt, and its description marks every login requirement as either formally verified or empirically checked. 

Merging is where the proof joins the team’s normal workflow. PDD Kit’s pdd-ship workflow adds the Verus check to CI next to the empirical tests, so every later change to login, by a person or an agent, has to keep proving against the same spec, and a broken proof fails the build like a failing test. And because a proof covers every input, PDD Kit prunes tests that only re-check what’s already proved, such as example-based tests of the password gate, and keeps the ones that guard the trusted boundary, so CI gets stronger and leaner at the same time. 

What the proof does and doesn’t say 

“Fully verified” is easy to oversell, so here’s exactly what we’re claiming.

  • Proved. The bodies of login_flow, login_core, lookup_target, decide_login and issue_token meet their contracts for every input. Login picks the right table, compares the request’s password against the stored hash of the account it names, issues a token with that account’s id and the role its table gives, and refuses everything else with today’s 400, 401 or 500 and no token. 
  • Trusted and tested. The two database lookups, check_password over bcrypt, the clock, token signing, the database error message and the handler’s request unpacking sit outside the proof, each behind an assumed contract the developer accepted. Tests against the real bcrypt, the real SQLite schema and the real router cover them. 
  • Assumed. The Verus, Rust compiler and Z3 (opens in new tab) toolchain, and Verus’s standard library vstd (opens in new tab). 

Why Rust 

PDD Kit only verifies Rust today, since that’s the language Verus works on. If your codebase is already Rust, there’s nothing to migrate. Code in other languages can be ported to Rust and checked against the same spec, and non-Rust projects can call verified Rust through bindings. 

There’s also a less obvious upside. Once reliance on exhaustive line-by-line review has been reduced, readability stops being the main reason to pick a language. You can pick one for speed and safety, and optimize as hard as you want, because any change that breaks the spec fails the proof. 

What to Expect from PDD Kit

PDD Kit is a research prototype, and it only verifies Rust today since that’s the language Verus works on. Code in other languages can be ported to Rust and checked against the same spec, and non-Rust projects can call verified Rust through bindings. Proofs still take real effort, mostly in producing the proof itself, and a clear spec is what keeps that effort down, which is why so much of PDD Kit is about getting intent right first. We’d start where a bug costs the most, such as login, payments, or permissions, and verify the rest of a codebase one piece at a time.

Pet Store’s login is one piece of one app: a spec anyone can read, a Verus proof that the code matches it, and tests for everything the proof takes on trust. We want to be upfront about the weakest links. The guarantees are only as strong as the six trusted pieces, and two carry most of the weight: check_password for every password promise, and the two lookups for every promise about which account a token names. Tests support them, but nothing proves them. We expect that trusted boundary to shrink significantly over time, so a growing share of the code can be formally verified, and we want to find out how far this scales.

What we’re really changing is what people review. Instead of relying mainly on line-by-line review of agent-generated code, a team reviews what it meant, in plain language, and a proof holds the code to it. The plan was always supposed to be the contract, and now the agent actually has to keep it.

Acknowledgments

This work is a collaboration between the Microsoft Research Catalyst Lab, GitHub Next, and the Research in Software Engineering (RiSE) group. We would like to thank Maggie Appleton and Krzysztof Cieślak of GitHub Next for their collaboration on Chopin, and Nikhil Swamy, Lef Ioannidis, Janardhan Kulkarni, and Shuvendu Lahiri for their feedback and discussions on formal verification and intent formalization. We also thank the F*/Pulse and Verus teams for their support. Finally, we thank Idan Gazit of GitHub Next for supporting this collaboration.

FAQ

  • You do, and yes, it would. A proof shows the code meets the spec, not that the spec is what you meant. That’s why PDD Kit is built around existing research in intent formalization. The pdd-plan workflow reads your code, asks questions before writing anything, and turns your answers into a Verus spec plus a plain-language plan you approve, flagging ambiguity instead of guessing. Two reviewer agents check the spec, and the pdd-prove workflow plants one bug per clause to catch clauses that verify but rule out nothing. A wrong spec is still possible, which is why PDD Kit emphasizes making requirements explicit, identifying ambiguities, and keeping developers involved in reviewing and approving the spec before verification begins. 

  • The difference is what holds the code to the plan.

    PDD keeps the planning loop from SDD and still uses tests where a proof can’t reach. A test checks some inputs, while a proof establishes that the code satisfies specified properties for all inputs covered by the formal model, under its stated assumptions. 

  • The proof is Rust code annotated with Verus constructs, checked mechanically by Verus using the Z3 solver. It runs wherever your Rust builds: the pdd-prove workflow runs it while proving, and the pdd-ship workflow adds it to your build and CI so a broken proof fails the build. The check is deterministic, with no model involved. Models write the spec, code, and proof, but only a deterministic Verus run decides whether it passed. How long the check takes varies with the size of the code and how hard the proofs are: usually seconds for a small module, up to minutes for a larger codebase.

  • PDD Kit shifts more of the review process toward validating what the code should do, while using formal verification to provide additional assurance that the implementation meets those requirements. Developers review the natural-language plan, the formal spec, and the trusted components that fall outside the scope of the proof. The resulting pull request documents what was formally verified, what was tested, and where additional review may be needed. On the Pet Store full stack web app, this approach reduced reliance on exhaustive line-by-line review of the generated code.

  • We chose Verus because it allows us to verify Rust code directly, aligning with PDD Kit’s focus on integrating formal verification into existing Rust development workflows. Other proof languages (e.g., Lean, F*, Rocq) take different approaches to formal verification, each with its own tradeoffs. The techniques behind PDD Kit could help put them to work as well.

item.title: Learn the rules: The hacker mindset
item.dc:creator: Weishung Liu, Mike Walker
item.description:
Research Manager Mike Walker reflects on a career spanning hacker culture, cybersecurity, and AI, sharing lessons about trust, teamwork, leadership, and why solving difficult problems requires curiosity, judgment, agility—and an understanding of the rules.

The post Learn the rules: The hacker mindset appeared first on Microsoft Research.
item.content:encoded:
For some, rules pose limitations. For others, like Microsoft Research Manager Mike Walker, they’re opportunities. 

Walker’s fascination with rules and their role in the social order has allowed him to find success professionally and personally, from uncovering weaknesses in networked systems to redefining how computers are trained to fend off cyberattacks to pushing the limits of a reliable mode of transportation—the bicycle—in ultra-endurance racing. 

In this conversation with Principal Technical Program Manager Weishung Liu, Walker describes how his participation in hacker culture led him to a career building next-generation cyber defense, including his work developing the first all-machine hacking tournament. Along the way, he reflects on why effective security depends on understanding trust and context, what competitive hacking taught him about teamwork and collective intelligence, and how an early lesson reshaped his understanding of leadership. He also tackles an important question: are today’s networked systems any safer than they were a decade ago?

Transcript 

[MUSIC] 

MIKE WALKER: Well, you have to understand the rules if you want to be able to do what you want. So I have, I have a definite fascination with the rules, [LAUGHTER] but the thing you have to understand about the rules is that rules are a social construct. And I think that a lot of … in the computer security field, when, when people hear the word “security” and they think about the rules that the security system is imposing on them, every time a security system asks something of users, then you’re asking for their trust. And that trust is a precious commodity. And so when you squander user trust, then the security regime falls down. So I think it’s really important to understand the social context of rules instead of just having instant adjudication. 

[THEME MUSIC] 

STANDARD INTRODUCTION: This is the Microsoft Research Podcast, where Microsoft researchers—driving advancement through fundamental science and technology research—explore the who, how, and what’s next in computing and AI.

[MUSIC ENDS] 

WEISHUNG LIU: Hi, and welcome. My name is Weishung Liu, and I’m a principal technical program manager here at Microsoft Research. And today, I’m joined by Mike Walker, who is a research manager here in MSR, or Microsoft Research, where he leads projects at the intersection of AI, cybersecurity, and large distributed systems. 

Before Microsoft, Mike led DARPA’s Cyber Grand Challenge, the pioneering program that demonstrated autonomous AI systems capable of finding and patching software vulnerabilities. And CGC actually just celebrated its 10th anniversary this year in 2026. 

Mike’s work spans groundbreaking efforts that include cloud native memory analysis, automated malware analysis, and next-generation cyber defense technologies. 

Mike, thanks for joining me. 

MIKE WALKER: Good to be here, Wei. 

LIU: All right, so, Mike, we have known each other for a couple of years now. And I’ve heard, like, bits and pieces of your story over time as we’ve gotten to talk. But before I really knew who you were, sort of, as a person, I, kind of, knew you as, like, “Mike Walker, the hacker guy that’s working over there,” which I’m sure you love. And I know you love that, when I call you “The Hacker.” 

But you’ve worked on so many things that I’ve never really thought about before. Like, new words have entered my vocabulary as a result of knowing you and working with you, like threat intelligence, nation states, and I think there are a couple other ones that I think would have never been in my lexicon had I not known you. 

So I’m hoping we can spend this time to also have the audience get to know you, as well. So we’re going to start at the beginning then. And the beginning is, I believe, Mike, you grew up in Ohio. 

WALKER: Columbus, Ohio. 

LIU: Columbus, Ohio. What kind of a kid were you in Columbus, Ohio? 

WALKER: I think I was a kid who spent a lot of time in the woods. [LAUGHTER] I was a skateboard kid. I was a basketball kid. But I think mostly I was a kid who read books and lived in a world of their own imagination. 

LIU: Were you on a farm in Columbus, Ohio, or were you in, like, or is this more suburban, rural, urban? 

WALKER: It was halves and halves. I spent my … most of the year in Columbus, Ohio, and then every summer, I would go out to the town of Tappahannock on the Rappahannock River in Virginia. And I lived completely on the farm. 

LIU: So what was the lifestyle in what you were doing different between, like, Columbus, Ohio, and the farm? 

WALKER: So, like, some things that I was doing in Columbus, Ohio, is that my father, who was sort of half scientist, half venture capitalist, would bring me home industrial equipment and say, “See what you can make out of this,” and drop it in my room. [LAUGHTER] Really dangerous stuff. And he would always give me safety warnings, right, like, “This is a helium neon laser.” You know, “This is … this tube is made out of glass. Don’t break it.” And then, “This is a really, really high-voltage power supply driving it, and it can arc and kill you,” right. And I knew what that meant. [LAUGHTER] And then he would leave me with it. And what can you make out of this, right. 

So I would do stuff like, like try to replicate the Michelson-Morley experiment, you know, because I had the, had the table and the mirrors and I could do that. And then also I spent a lot of time with the Apple II, which was this just incredible machine from some other universe that I had never gone to. I later found out that was, you know, hackerspace and, and information technology culture, but it came from nowhere and there was nobody I could talk to about it. And so I spent a lot of time trying to hook the Apple II up to stuff in my life and, and try to control it with that thing. 

LIU: OK, so you brought up some hacker stuff, so I have to ask. There was farm stuff. There was, you know, “dad brought home interesting tools and equipment.” How did all of that get you interested in cybersecurity? 

WALKER: I think I was always in cybersecurity. I just didn’t know. 

LIU: Explain. 

WALKER: You know, there’s this idea that you live two lives: the one before you find out your purpose and the one after you find it. This was, sort of, life before purpose, where I didn’t know why I was so interested in how these things worked. 

So, you know, I ran a bulletin board system. Before the internet, this was how computers communicated with each other. Dial-up modems, not even backbone linked. Each, each BBS—bulletin board system—[LAUGHTER] was, was a universe unto itself, you know, architected by its creator. And so there were all these little universes you could dial into. And then at some point, all these things I’d been doing my whole life, sort of, got connected to a career. 

When you say, you know, somebody could, right, somebody could listen to every single badge swipe event on the network, on campus, and then replicate them and badge themselves into any building they wanted because this is all in a broadcast LAN [local area network] and somebody should change that, there was a time when if you said things like that, the people you told it to would just be like, “Well, don’t do that,” [LAUGHTER] right? And then … 

LIU: Did you listen to them? 

WALKER: No. [LAUGHTER] I was young. 

Um, and then at some point, the world started getting serious about imposing rules onto networked computers, and they started hiring people who are interested in that. And that’s … suddenly it was a career, right. I was like, “Oh, I was always here, but now it has a name.” 

LIU: So I have to ask then, like, you brought up the notion of rules. I feel like cybersecurity and rules has a relationship there. How much of a rule follower were you growing up versus how much do you think you are a rule follower now, and was there a difference or have you always been some version of “rule following”? 

WALKER: Well, you have to understand the rules if you want to be able to do what you want. 

LIU: Yes. 

WALKER: So I have a definite fascination with the rules, [LAUGHTER] but the thing you have to understand about the rules is that rules are a social construct. And I think that a lot of … in the computer security field, when, when people hear the word “security” and they think about the rules that the security system is imposing on them, every time a security system asks something of users, then you’re asking for their trust. And that trust is a precious commodity. And so when you squander user trust, then the security regime falls down. So I think it’s really important to understand the social context of rules instead of just having instant adjudication. 

LIU: OK. I’m going to have to ask you then about a game that we played recently called No Vehicles in the Park (opens in new tab). 

WALKER: No Vehicles in the Park is … it’s a game about content moderation is one way to look at it. I think it’s a fascinating thought experiment. But it just takes the thesis that rules are simple and challenges it with putting the player in the position of judge. And so the name of the exercise is the name of the rule, which is no vehicles in the park. 

And then it asks you some very simple commonsense questions about, is this a violation of the rule no vehicles in the park? Like if the International Space Station overflies the park, is that a vehicle in the park, and is it against the rules? 

LIU: Mike, do you think the ISS flying over the park is a violation of the rules? 

WALKER: No. [LAUGHTER] But it’s important that we have a resilient way to adjudicate things that, that bridges social norms. 

LIU: OK. How much did you agree with the population, by the way, of No Vehicles in the Park? 

WALKER: I’ve rarely ever broken 50%. Yeah. 

LIU: I got like 90 … 

WALKER: I play often. 

LIU: I think I got 96% on my first try, so I think I … does that mean I’m kind of like a lemming that, like, just understands the social construct of rules? 

WALKER: I think it means you, you channel the zeitgeist. 

LIU: Mm, OK, I’ve been assimilated. 

WALKER: Right … 

LIU: That’s what it feels like. 

All right. So let’s talk about something that I love, which is you had a short segment in 60 Minutes (opens in new tab) where you had a conversation with Lesley Stahl, and she described you as “one of the world’s top hackers,” at least at the time in which she interviewed you. And so now I have to know, how did you find hacker cultures? What was the extent of your involvement and, you know, how did you really get into it? 

WALKER: It, sort of, happened all at once, and I can tell the beginning of the story, and then I can tell you the day that the story stops. 

So the beginning of the story is that I was working at a, at a startup building telecommunications technologies on Sept. 11, 2001, and I was living in Maryland, outside of Washington, D.C., but my wife was in Washington, D.C., on that day, and, um, and then all the phones stopped working. My workplace was overflown by an F-16, and, and after that, in the nation’s capital, there was this sudden talent search for people who understood computer security or people who’d always been there but didn’t know what it was called. And that talent search found me. 

LIU: What, uh, what were the qualifications, like, that you had that, you know, matched with their list of talent that they were looking for? 

WALKER: I wish I knew. 

LIU: World’s top hacker? 

WALKER: I think, I think that that label was placed on me much later. 

LIU: [LAUGHS] All right, fine. 

WALKER: I think that I became part of a series of cultures after that day, and one of them was the, the group of people who play in DEF CON Capture the Flag, which is a hacking contest in Las Vegas. And when you start getting involved in trying to get, get better at something in a way where you can compete at a national or international level, especially in sort of a coffeehouse environment where everyone else is trying to get better, too, it sort of propels you upward very quickly. 

LIU: OK, let’s, let’s go back later to talk about Capture the Flag, because I think it’s related to the, sort of, next arc of your life, which was your time as a project manager—program manager—at the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, also known as DARPA, which is also why Lesley had been interviewing you at the time. It was associated with your affiliation at DARPA, and you were there for about four years. 

How did you, how did you go from, you know, let’s say call, call to action from the nation’s capital looking for people with your specific set of skills to being at DARPA as a PM. 

WALKER: So we should, we should be clear, we’ve just, sort of, skipped over 11 years of Mike trying to get better at hacking. 

LIU: [LAUGHS] You were world’s top—look, I just believe world’s top hacker, one of the world’s top hackers. 

WALKER: Well, I think, uh, I think my, my friends, colleagues, and teammates from the time, if they were here to, to hear that accusation being made, would give me endless grief about it. 

Certainly, there was a, there was, sort of, a golden age of Capture the Flag, and I got to be part of it and see some of the people. I got to see the game change over time. But it was a competition, so … and it was very reflective of a skill set that was of national interest. I think at the same time, the think tank RAND had published an opinion piece called Hackers Wanted (opens in new tab), right, which, sort of, described the immense need for more people who could think that way at a high level. 

And DARPA, specifically Norm Whitaker and Dan Kaufman, who were leading I2O [Information Innovation Office] … 

LIU: DARPA Dan! 

WALKER: DARPA Dan … looked at the game of hackers, right, and if you could think of that as soccer, their immediate question was, what about robot soccer? You know, could we make automated systems that could play this game? And so they encountered myself and some colleagues giving a talk about, sort of, the, the interleaving of Capture the Flag as, you know, hacking contests and talent development. And they said, you know, could you do talent development for computers the same way, right? Could machines play Capture the Flag? And that, that was the beginning of the conversation about building the world’s first all-machine hacking tournament. 

LIU: OK, so now, now maybe let’s go back and explain what DEF CON Capture the Flag was, or CTF, because I think a lot of us who are again not in the space, you say, “Capture the Flag,” and I’m thinking, like, summer camp. And, you know, each … there are two teams, and there’s kids who hide flags, and then you try to run around and find the flag, you find the defenders and whatnot. So what was the DEF CON version of this? 

WALKER: It’s changed over time. That’s the thing about this game that I should lead with is that Capture the Flag is different with every generation, and at least in my opinion, I think it’s gotten better with every generation, right. Each hacking group that’s picked up the lessons of the past and the game has made it better, but it is, sort of, based around that playground idea, right. My team has some flags. Your team has some flags. We’re going to try to take each other’s flags. Whoever takes the most wins, right. It is that simple. 

Now there are more than two teams, somewhere between eight and 16, and each team is trying to take flags from every other team. They’re trying to protect their own flags. But, of course, the flags are made of data, right, … 

LIU: Mm-hm. 

WALKER: … or control over a networked system. And the way that you protect your own data and control of your own network system is network defense, right, and computer defense. And the way that you take flags from other, other teams is you hack into their servers and you take their flags and you do it without getting caught. And then what makes this game, sort of, unique is that all the software that you’re protecting is written just for that game. It will never be used again. It’s boutique. It was written by the organizers, kept in secret, revealed to the teams the minute they sit down. They’ve got new software they’ve never seen before. They don’t know what it does, and they’re in a race to understand it, and they’re racing everybody else. Because if you can understand it, then you can protect it, and if you can understand it, you can hack it. 

LIU: OK. So let’s get into this thing called DARPA’s Cyber Grand Challenge, or CGC, which just celebrated its 10th anniversary. And so from what I understand, CTF—humans playing soccer. CGC … robots playing soccer? Is that probably a good way to, to … 

WALKER: That’s exactly it. 

LIU: OK, so now explain to me a little bit further, like, what was CGC, what was your role, and then more importantly, did it feel historic at the time or just, kind of, impossible and you somehow figured out with a large group of folks at DARPA, “This is how we’re going to solve this impossible thing”? 

WALKER: Well, there’s, there’s two ways to answer that. There’s the, the day before it worked and the day after it worked, right. [LAUGHTER] There were actually three and a half years before it worked. So if you’d ask me, I think, in any of that three and a half years, I would have said let’s wait and see. 

LIU: So, so what was it, though, like—by the way, I think you can watch the first CGC online (opens in new tab). Like, there’s a whole recording of the event. 

WALKER: There is a recording of the event, which we had sports casted live with announcers, and, and so you can watch it as it happened, and it was, it was a capture the flag, right—protect data, steal data—that was run entirely by autonomous systems behind an air gap, so if they failed, there was no person even to turn them off and turn them back on again. 

LIU: So how did … so if I think about how you just described Capture the Flag with DEF CON, but there were, like, people on the floor coding, I’m assuming, though, you’re saying CGC did not have that. So were there teams that had, like, pre-created something? 

WALKER: Yes. They had spent many years of their life actually building these autonomous systems, and you can’t really preflight an autonomous system whose purpose is to fight. You can preflight an autonomous system whose purpose is to maybe go for a drive, right. You can take it for a drive. But if you’re going to fight other systems, you have to, like, build another one, right. And we did give them some exposure to a, sort of, scripted opponent. 

The DARPA infrastructure team built a scripted opponent and attempted to give teams some pre-exposure. But that first confrontation between adversarial hacking machines, there wasn’t really a great way to prepare for it. And so the teams were in this really tough position of watching the systems play—win or lose—in a way where they couldn’t do anything but watch. 

LIU: So, you know, I want you to think back on that time, as well, because, like, now when we’re talking about AI, it seems a little bit more commonplace, right? We’re like, oh, you know, we have GPT, we have Claude, we have a lot of other models, as well. So, like, how historic was that? Because I think it can’t be understated how vastly different, sort of, autonomous or artificial intelligence capabilities were like 10 years ago versus now. 

WALKER: It was, it was a different universe of capability, and Cyber Grand Challenge had a role in the development of the technology stacks that we’re seeing today, but it was an expert systems contest. There was, there was no—at that time, we would have called it machine learning—but there’s no, no real involvement, critical involvement, in machine learning. 

But there was this fusion of tooling where you had, sort of, an autonomous set of tools that could perform a lot of these tasks as far as conventional compute could push the state of the practice at the time. I think if we look back from the perspective of today, which is, which is still a perspective that’s difficult to keep up with and difficult to appreciate how, how radically different the intelligence displayed by today’s models is from what we had in 2013, 2016, we’re still seeing the technology stacks that we would have called “expert systems” in 2016 being used as what we call a harness today. 

So if … just to talk about another DARPA project, AIxCC [AI Cyber Challenge] (opens in new tab), which happened a few years ago, some of the people from Team Atlanta, which won that competition (opens in new tab), are building a harness called MDASH, which is, I think we could call it a cyber reasoning system that is powered by models and used to do these sorts of tasks autonomously. 

LIU: You were interviewed by The New York Times in 2016 about CGC (opens in new tab), and you said that making networked technology safer was a “challenge for civilization.” And, you know, what do you think about that? Has civilization made progress on, you know, resolving that challenge? And what are some tangible takeaways that you think, you know, from 10 years ago till now, think through sort of how, how we’re making things safer for civilization? 

WALKER: I’d say that’s as true now as it was then, maybe more so. And I think our dependence on networked systems for every piece of civilization has only increased. I think it’s difficult to buy a car or to participate in a utility grid that isn’t networked, right. 

How we’re doing? I think that we’re seeing a great disruption of the status quo right now. I think that we reached a pretty steady-state equilibrium, where our, our security in our networked civilization was, sort of, dictated by offensive scarcity. There was a known cost for high-end computer network attack, and that cost equation has been completely upended by the capabilities of models. 

LIU: So in thinking about, sort of, capabilities of models then, some terms that, that I’ve heard used are things when we’re testing models, for example, is––we call it––red teaming. But then I also hear that there’s something called blue teaming. And then, of course, if you’ve taken primary colors or understood kindergarten primary colors, if you put red and blue together, you get purple teaming. Can you explain to the audience a little bit about those differences? 

WALKER: Yeah. Red team and blue team is sort of an artificial separation between being an attacker and being a defender, and it’s also, sort of, an oversimplification and an abnegation of capability, right. Attackers attack; defenders defend. But if you, if you take that simplification away and you look at what’s going on under the hood, you’ll see that the difference between offense and defense most of the time is, sort of, who’s in control or who’s driving. 

If you were to give a name to a program that encrypted every file in your computer and then unlocked it when you needed it, that is either a cryptography utility or it’s ransomware depending on who holds the key. If you were to give a name to a program that, that allows you to log in to your computer remotely and control it, maybe your home automation setup, that is either malware or remote administration utility [LAUGHTER] depending on who holds the key, right? Who holds the key. 

So there’s, there’s this, sort of, blurring of offense and defense where computer security capabilities at their most atomic basic level aren’t offensive or defensive. They’re dual use. And so the idea of red teaming and blue teaming is sort of this idea that we can impose single use onto dual-use capabilities, and purple team is the acknowledgment that that’s not true, right. 

Attackers, as soon as they break into a network, they have an intrusion that they need to defend. You’ll hear all these terms like moving laterally, which just means breaking into more computers, or exfiltration, which means taking data. But the whole time they’re doing that, they’re trying not to get caught, right. So they are defending their attack, right. 

LIU: Mm. 

WALKER: And at the same time, when defenders are doing things like log analysis or really any—or traffic analysis—their tools themselves can be broken into, right. They have a duty to defend their own tooling, and they also need to, in order to prevent attackers, they need to be able to find vulnerabilities, find weaknesses, and then grade weaknesses in their own software. And the way that you find vulnerabilities is vulnerability research, and you grade weaknesses by writing exploits or at least proof of vulnerability, and that’s offense, right. So purple team is just this idea that attack and defense are the same skill set. They’re the same tooling. They’re blended. And it’s really a contest to control the logic of memory of networked computers run all the time. 

LIU: All right. So, so I’m going to ask you a little bit about the team that you manage then. It’s called New Security Ventures. And would you classify the type of work that you and your team do as being red, blue, or purple? Or are we going to introduce a different coloring from the rainbow? 

WALKER: I think that we do highly offense-aware defensive tool development. So we build defensive tools, but we build them knowing that they are a target. 

LIU: What’s one example of a project that your team has been working on? 

WALKER: We have a project we call Project Freta. It’s named after the birthplace of Marie Curie (opens in new tab), the pioneer of battlefield imaging (opens in new tab). [LAUGHTER] And the idea is, is that … well, first I actually need to introduce tampering. We think of ourselves as the solution to tampering, but, but first, what’s tampering, right? 

LIU: What’s tampering?

WALKER: What problem are we solving?

So let’s say that my job is to break into a store undiscovered, right? It’s mission impossible, right? I’m going to break in, take the Doritos, not get caught, right. 

 LIU: Wait. Hold on. What flavor of Doritos? 

 WALKER: I don’t know. 

 LIU: What?! 

WALKER: I don’t actually eat them. I’m sorry. 

LIU: OK, fine. 

WALKER: But that’s, you know, it’s mission impossible. I have to take them. 

LIU: Fine. You got to go get Doritos. 

WALKER: I have to not show up on the video. 

LIU: Yeah. 

WALKER: I can compute this path of not being observed by the video camera. It’s really hard, right. Maybe I do some, some kung fu, some gymnastics. I slide into the laser wire, I grab it, and I get out. But there is another way to break in and not get caught, which is to walk in, right, wave at the camera, cut the feed on the camera, take it down, and replace it with a fake video camera that just plays good video, like there’s nobody in the, in the store, and then go in and change the tape and leave. That’s tampering, right? 

LIU: OK. 

WALKER: And it sounds actually less complicated, right, than trying to simply not be observed. And if you look in the computer security world at tampering, tampering is often the easier way to accomplish the objective of an attacker, which is to break in and not get caught and defend their intrusion, right. They’re doing defense while they’re doing offense. And so Project Freta is an attempt to solve that at cloud scale, to make it so that when defenders acquire defensive signals, right, telemetry signals about what’s happening in computers, they don’t do it with software that can be removed or tampered with. They do it by acquiring signals from cloud hardware. And so we’re a whole-system memory analysis environment built from the ground up for looking at memory that’s acquired from cloud hardware. 

LIU: So, OK, so you just revealed, for example, how Project Freta works and how it protects or is trying to defend against something like tamper. But then, you know, I’m kind of curious, though. You just revealed how it works. So, you know, you’re kind of telling the attackers what you’re doing and how you’re defending. How does that work if you’re like, “This is how I’m defending, like, this is how I’m defending my castle. Here you go”? 

WALKER: Well, you can reveal a technology or you can reveal its deployment. And I’ve revealed a technology, and I haven’t said anything about its deployment. 

LIU: OK, so there’s a, there’s a difference, and there’s layers that you’ve described so that, you know, even though you’ve revealed something, you haven’t revealed the full extent. 

WALKER: Well, you’re, you’re bringing up a really interesting part of the game theory of, of adversarial computer network attack-computer network defense, which is that attackers condition their behavior based on their perception of what the defense is doing. And so that gets into these, these strange effects of, is the best way to protect a network to say that you have something or to actually have it or to have a mismatch between what you say you have and what you have. 

LIU: So you’re like bluffing in poker. 

WALKER: There’s a reason this game is played in Vegas. [LAUGHTER] 

LIU: OK, OK. So we’ve had, we’ve had some, like, more serious, like, topics for a while. And I want to get into something that maybe a lot of folks who maybe even know you don’t know about you, which is you love—I think I’m going to use … I think I can say love—cycling. 

WALKER: That’s true. 

LIU: How did you get into cycling? 

WALKER: I got into cycling in, sort of, the way that I’ve gotten into a lot of things in my life, which is I got into it through what I thought at the time was, was a disaster. I blew out my knee playing basketball, which was one of my first great loves, right. And I went through surgical repair. And afterwards, the surgeon told me you can’t do the stuff with this knee that you used to do. 

I said, “Well, what can I do?” You know, I hadn’t even thought to ask this question before surgery. You know, I’m sitting there trying to, like, rehabilitate the knee. And he said, “Well, you could try swimming or you could try riding a bike.” 

I didn’t really know anything about either one. You know, I used to ride a bike to get around. And then a friend of mine in college introduced me to mountain biking, which is sort of this idea that you could take a bicycle, which is a very stable system—you know, you go out and you ride it down the sidewalk; it works great—and ride it over, you know, just horrible, you know, really steep, rough terrain that no one should ever try to ride a bike on. 

LIU: OK. And you did this recently at a 100-mile endurance race called High Cascades. 

WALKER: High Cascades 100 (opens in new tab). 

LIU: And what was it like to prep for that? Because I feel like you’ve been, you’ve been working on some very important things on the professional side. And then you also had this big 100-mile endurance race that you were prepping for on the personal side. How did that go? 

WALKER: There are very few things in life where you have a fixed date and time where you have to show up and deal with uncertainty, and ultra-endurance racing is one of those. Um, there’s, there’s the parts that you can prepare for and the parts you can’t, right. You can’t prepare for the smoke forecast or the weather. You can just have a range of options. 

But then, you know, as far as the conditioning, I do spend a lot of time on the indoor trainer. I just wake up really early. I have, I have a whole structured plan. I think I started around January to race in July. 

LIU: Do you follow them like you follow rules? [LAUGHS] 

WALKER: Well, I’m much more strict about following my training plan. Actually, I think, I think I’ve been advised—this is real—not to be trainer robot. 

LIU: Wow. 

WALKER: So I had to back off on being trainer robot. 

LIU: OK, so you had to ease up on the rules that you were following, that you wrote for yourself. 

WALKER: Yeah. There’s this mode … all the cycling fans on the … watching this are going to, are going to be like, [WHISPERS] “Oh my gosh, he’s talking about erg mode.” There’s this mode called erg mode where the, the trainer decides how hard you should pedal. And it took me … and so I would just set it to that and do what it told me, right. And so it was this big thing to, to actually go into free ride and try to, try to ride the terrain. 

LIU: OK. 

WALKER: Yeah. Back, back off and try to, try to listen to your body a little bit rather than just do whatever it takes. 

LIU: [LAUGHS] I feel like there’s a relationship between what we are talking about now and something maybe related to the cybersecurity side of Mike. But I have to … I really want to get a photo of this on this podcast, this video podcast. So I am going to ask you about Orange Crush. 

WALKER: Oh, OK. 

LIU: Can you tell the audience, what is Orange Crush? 

WALKER: Orange Crush is the project bike that I built over the year when I was out with a blown shoulder. 

LIU: I think that’s when I met you. 

WALKER: Yeah. The problem with riding the bikes down the steep hills is, like, sometimes, it doesn’t go completely perfect. 

LIU: Didn’t we have … we also had a colleague who also likes to mountain bike who, like, broke his back at around the same time you had a shoulder injury. 

WALKER: Yeah. 

LIU: Also mountain biking. 

WALKER: Yeah. Kind of depends on how you break your back versus how you break your shoulder on which one of those works out better. 

I got a … I messed my shoulder up pretty good, so it took some time, but it meant that I got to, kind of, conceive of something and put it together, mostly left-handed, which is its own challenge. So it’s, it’s a gravel bike, but it’s … and, of course, my wife named it. She gets the naming rights because she’s better at it, but it is very orange. 

LIU: Um, we’re, we’re coming up close on time, so I’m going to start wrapping up with a few questions, but I, I love this question and I can’t help but ask you, Mike, what is the difference between suffering on a bike and suffering through a hard technical project? 

WALKER: Well, I don’t think of riding a bike as suffering at all. That’s like the good part. 

LIU: Even, even, OK. Because in your 100-mile endurance race on High Cascades, I think you said it was, like, nine hours of … 

WALKER: Yeah. 

LIU: … nonstop riding, like, in terrain. 

WALKER: Racing. Yeah. 

LIU: That seems like there might have been a little bit of suffering. 

WALKER: No, that’s absolutely the best part. [LAUGHTER] No, no, the suffering is, the suffering is the checklist and the logistics the day before. Suffering is going out for a pre- ride and getting a flat and trying to find a bike shop that can get a tire patch in the day before High Cascades. [LAUGHTER] No, the logistics and the, and the worrying, right, that’s always the hard part. Once, once, once you’re at … you know, it just gets worse and worse up until the start. And then you’re racing, and it’s wonderful. 

LIU: And I want the audience to know—because High Cascades, you can actually look it up on the internet … 

WALKER: That’s true. 

LIU: … Mike finished 69th out of 329 participants (opens in new tab). I’d say that’s pretty, that’s pretty darn good. I don’t even know how to ride a bike, Mike. 

WALKER: Um, I, I race these days to learn about myself, you know. 

LIU: Do you work on hard technical projects to also learn about yourself? 

WALKER: I work on hard technical projects half because just getting to solve hacking problems is, it’s, sort of, what I’ve always done. But then also, I get to work with great people, and I get to, I get to see impact. I get to see the impact of our work. 

LIU: All right. So I have a lightning round of questions that I’m going to ask you. 

WALKER: OK. All right. 

LIU: So just come up with—this is not a Rorschach test. Just come up with, like, … 

WALKER: It might be. 

LIU: It requires pictures if I do that. But we’re going to do a lightning round. So the first one: advice that blew your mind or changed your perspective. 

WALKER: Hm, um, I remember when I was starting at the agency, I was, I’d, I’d worked in an engineering shop for a long time, and the culture of, of many engineering shops is to be critical of leadership, right. They would see what leadership did and then take the information they had and be critical of the decision. Not all the time, but sometimes. And I had a mentor who took me aside and said, “Have you ever considered that the decisions that you don’t agree with are the result of information you don’t have?” 

LIU: Ooh. 

WALKER: And then they took me into a situation where I, sort of, was revealed … the, the information I didn’t have about the decision I disagreed with was revealed to me, and suddenly I thought it was a great decision. I was like, “That’s incredible.” And then I left and I couldn’t talk about it, and I saw other people having the same criticism of the decision, and that started the process of reformatting how I thought about leadership. Every time I hear a decision now, I think to myself, “What do they know that I don’t?” And that curiosity process is always running. 

LIU: OK. Lesson you learned the hard way—which is … I feel like this is a very easy question for you—or the misstep that humbled you. 

WALKER: There’s so much to choose from here. [LAUGHTER] 

LIU: First one that comes to mind. 

WALKER: I probably made one on the way here. 

I’ll, I’ll pick one that’s, that’s relevant to the discussion today, which is that I remember distinctly playing in qualifiers in a hacking competition and getting, getting the answer, right—getting the key, right—and running up to the person who was handing in keys for our team, being like, “I solved”— you know, I don’t know what it was; every challenge has a name, right—”like, 202,” and they were like, “Oh, we solved that an hour and a half ago.” [LAUGHTER] 

And, and I, I remember, you know, “Oh, OK. Well, I better find something new to work on.” And I just looked around the room and, you know, we’re all curled over our hacking workstations, two monitors and a keyboard no one would recognize as a keyboard—you know, we all look the same—and, and thinking to myself, I can quantify the IQ in this room, but I can’t look around and quantify how well we’re working together. 

LIU: Mmm.

WALKER: Right? I don’t know how aligned we are in this goal of getting the most points and winning here. And I can’t look around and figure out how many people here are on the right challenge or on a challenge that’s already been solved, have the tools they need, would be paired with the right person. 

And myself and a couple of my colleagues started thinking about, like, what is the right way to create social intelligence in, in technical teams and hacking teams? And, and that has stuck with me. I mean, that’s been a constant thread, is, is just the abandonment of the hero journey and net IQ as a way that, that teams accomplish things, because you will find people working on challenges to get the key, right—as a metaphor—where the problem’s already been solved in any organization that isn’t working on, on its EQ. You’ll find it everywhere. 

LIU: OK, talent or—I was going to ask you a bunch more, but we’re lightning rounding right now. Talent or accomplishment you’re most proud of if given the chance to brag. 

WALKER: Mm. Bragging’s not in my nature, I don’t think. But … 

LIU: I know. Which is the … 

WALKER: But … 

LIU: Go on. 

WALKER: Let’s see. 

LIU: Flex a little bit. 

WALKER: I, uh, I taught myself to juggle while my knee was blown out. 

LIU: [LAUGHTER] That’s the thing you’re most proud of is juggling. 

WALKER: Well, so if you haven’t, if you haven’t learned how to juggle, it’s fine, right. But if you have, you know that 99% of it is dropping them and they go everywhere, which when you’re immobilized with a busted knee, it’s actually harder than it sounds. 

So I engineered a way to teach myself to juggle where I just got myself into a small enough space that I couldn’t lose them and I could just sit there with my blown-out post-surgery knee and teach myself to juggle. I did it in a couple of weeks. 

LIU: Can you still juggle? 

WALKER: Oh, yeah. 

LIU: OK, so if I handed you stuff later … 

WALKER: I mean, let’s not break the room, but sure. 

LIU: [LAUGHS] OK. Last one: career path you would have chosen—this is going to be hard—if you weren’t, like, in cybersecurity. And it feels like it’s, like, in your DNA, so I’m not sure, but I would love to hear an attempt. 

WALKER: Oh, it’s science fiction writer 100%. 

LIU: Really?

WALKER: You know, I thought I was going to be a musician, but when you’re a … when you go out and you start getting into a music scene, you, kind of, find out if you were a natural or not. So I think science fiction writer is still the thing where I wish I’d kept at it a little more. 

LIU: All right, I’m going to, I’m going to break my own rule, which is not … which is a social construct, and ask you one more, which is, can you recommend to the audience a really good—your favorite or one of the best sci-fi books you’ve ever read? 

WALKER: Oh, sure. Easy. It’s The Forever War (opens in new tab). Haldeman’s Forever War. And it’s, I think, it’s about coming to hand in the key except the challenge’s already solved, except sort of writ large in a, in a universe governed by relativity. 

 LIU: OK. 

 WALKER: No spoilers. 

 LIU: No spoilers. All right. Fine.

Thank you so much, Mike—this was a great time—for joining me.

To our audience, thank you for listening. If you want to learn a little bit more about any of my colleagues in Microsoft Research and their work, check out the Microsoft Research website at aka.ms/research (opens in new tab) [MUSIC] or listen and watch other episodes of the podcast on YouTube and major podcast platforms.
