item.title: From synthetic enterprise data evaluations to real Microsoft Copilot AI confidence
item.dc:creator: Somya Chatterjee, Harshita Sahijwani, Min Chen, Sushmitha Rajeswari Muppa, Dayquan Julienne, Irene Shaffer, Chandra Inguva, Jenny Chen, Minha Hwang, Sam Ade Jacobs
item.description:
Evaluating Microsoft Copilot at enterprise scale requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations, yet real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances.

The post From synthetic enterprise data evaluations to real Microsoft Copilot AI confidence appeared first on Microsoft Research.
item.content:encoded:
At a glance

  • Evaluating Microsoft Copilot at enterprise scale requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations, yet real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances.
  • To resolve this tension, we built Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform: full-scale synthetic enterprise environments grounded in publicly available real-world data sources such as O*NET occupational data, online job postings, and SEC filings.
  • The synthetic environments mimic real business workflows, helping Microsoft find issues that generic benchmarks would miss.
  • Safety and privacy are built into the platform by design. Every environment is fully synthetic and automated content-safety checks keep the generated data free of harmful or personally identifiable material.

Every day, millions of knowledge workers around the world rely on Microsoft Copilot to draft documents, summarize meetings, surface relevant information, and accelerate productivity. Behind the scenes, this is powered by a network of AI systems, and ensuring they work as intended requires a thoughtful approach to evaluation. At Microsoft, we know that high performance doesn’t come from guesswork. It comes from testing, measuring, and iterating constantly.

Healthcare organizations are constantly synthesizing safety signals from across teams so that they can make faster, better decisions that directly influence patient outcomes and regulatory confidence.

They may ask Copilot to summarize a meeting and extract action items for their teams. Within seconds, Copilot delivers a structured summary citing specific discussion points from the transcript. But how do we ensure this response is accurate, complete, and properly grounded in the meeting content? This is where our evaluation system comes in.

We’ve developed a structured evaluation strategy called Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform, which includes industry specific evaluation datasets designed to test AI systems against realistic enterprise scenarios, grounded in three core pillars:

  • Synthetic enterprise environments: simulated Microsoft Copilot environments with realistic users, meetings, emails, documents, and organizational structures that replicate the complexity of real organizations without using any customer data
  • Automated query generation pipelines for rapid, reproducible creation of evaluation datasets
  • Structured quality frameworks to ensure synthetic data meets the bar for meaningful evaluation

Together, these pillars help us answer two fundamental questions: Is Microsoft Copilot actually doing what our users need it to do, and can we prove it without ever touching their data?

In this blog post, we’ll walk through our evaluation system and processes, from synthetic environment generation to automated query pipelines, and how it all comes together to establish the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot.

Synthetic enterprise environments

Evaluating enterprise AI requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations: reporting structures, project histories, communication patterns, and domain specific workflows. But real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. This is the central tension we set out to resolve.

Rather than relying on small, manually curated test fixtures, we generate full scale synthetic environments: simulated enterprise workspaces, each with realistic organizational structures, communication histories, and work artifacts. In Microsoft terminology, each of these simulated workspaces is called a “tenant”. A tenant is an isolated organizational environment with its own users, data, and configurations. These environments are scalable baselines that teams and organizations can build off of however they want. They are designed to exhibit the same structural and behavioral properties that make enterprise AI evaluation meaningful.

Grounding in real world signals

To ensure our synthetic environments are realistic, we grounded them in publicly available real world data sources.

  • O*NET data from the U.S. Department of Labor’s occupational database was used to make synthetic employee roles and responsibilities realistic, calibrate the mix and frequency of work activities assigned to different roles, and tailor industry specific workflows such as clinical trial reviews or portfolio updates.
  • Online job postings provide realistic role titles, reporting hierarchies, and departmental compositions.
  • SEC filings inform organizational scale, business unit structures, and financial contexts. All of these sources are publicly available and have been reviewed and approved by Microsoft’s legal and policy organization.

Importantly, these synthetic environments are not static snapshots. They simulate dynamic, time-evolving organizations with meeting histories, project timelines, email threads that develop over weeks, and organizational changes that unfold naturally. This temporal dimension is essential because a large class of Copilot queries are inherently time aware. Questions like “What did the team decide last Thursday?” or “What’s changed since the last quarterly review?” only produce meaningful evaluations if the underlying data has a genuine temporal structure.

Industry specific simulation

We generated three synthetic environments across multiple industries, each with distinct characteristics that mirror real world usage:

  • A pharmaceutical environment that includes regulatory submission workflows, clinical trial discussions, and cross functional safety review meetings
  • A capital markets environment featuring deal pipelines, compliance communications, and client portfolio reviews
  • An IT/software company that simulates sprint planning, code review discussions, and product launch coordination

This industry specificity ensures that our evaluation queries test Copilot against the kinds of questions real users in those domains actually ask, rather than relying on generic test cases that may not surface domain specific failure modes.

Automated query generation

While synthetic environments provide the substrate for evaluation, they face a key limitation: we still need realistic evaluation queries. These are the questions that test whether Copilot can surface the right information, synthesize it correctly, and present it helpfully. Manually writing thousands of grounded, industry specific queries is prohibitively expensive and slow. That’s where our automated pipeline comes in.

The six-stage pipeline

We built an automated pipeline that turns simple, generic query ideas into realistic, industry-specific questions for Copilot. It starts with a large library of common workplace tasks, narrows them down to what’s relevant for a given industry, and adapts them using domain-specific language and context. The system then uses AI to generate queries grounded in the synthetic environment’s data, rewrites them to sound more natural and human, and validates each one for accuracy and uniqueness. The result is a rich set of high-quality, lifelike queries that enable scalable and reliable evaluation of Copilot across real-world scenarios.

Validating synthetic quality

Of course, generating synthetic data is only part of the challenge. We also need to ensure the data is good enough to produce meaningful evaluations. We assess synthetic environment quality using our internal semantic evaluation framework which measures quality across three dimensions:

  • Structural fidelity: Does the organizational structure reflect realistic reporting hierarchies, team sizes, and cross functional relationships?
  • Contextual relevance: Are the queries and workflows representative of actual enterprise usage patterns?
  • Behavioral realism: Do the simulated users exhibit human-like communication patterns and collaboration dynamics?
  • Content safety: Is the generated content free of harmful, offensive, or personally identifiable material, and does it avoid impersonating real individuals?

End-to-end automation

While our synthetic environments and query pipelines provide the methodology, they face several practical limitations without proper automation, including:

  • Reproducibility: Manual processes produce subtly different results each time, making it difficult to compare evaluations across releases.
  • Scale: The number of industry verticals and configuration variants exceeds what any team can reasonably produce by hand.
  • Iteration speed: Manual creation takes days, delaying essential feedback and slowing down development cycles.
  • Cross-team consistency: Without standardized tooling, different teams produce evaluation datasets with incompatible formats and quality levels.

This automation reduced evaluation dataset creation from a multi-day manual process to automated runs. We estimate savings of approximately $100,000 per evaluation dataset and $300,000 in total project savings. But the more important outcome is that any team can now regenerate an evaluation dataset from the same configuration and get identical results.

ACADEMIC CONFERENCE

Microsoft at SOSP 2026

Academic and industrial participants present research and experience papers that cover the full range of theory and practice of computer systems software.

Learn more
Opens in a new tab

Privacy and safety by design

Enterprise grade evaluation demands more than good methodology. It requires a privacy posture that allows teams to move fast without compromising user trust. A non-negotiable design principle of our industry evaluation datasets is that no real customer data is used at any stage of the pipeline. Every element, from organizational structures to email content to meeting transcripts, is synthetically generated, with no customer data inputs. Because the data is both fully synthetic and safety-screened, teams can share and reuse it widely without introducing reputational, compliance, or Responsible AI risk.

Our safeguards include privacy preserving aggregation techniques where real-world statistical distributions are referenced, expert legal review and approval of all public data sources, and clear data provenance and lineage tracking throughout the pipeline.

This means teams across Microsoft can use these evaluation datasets freely for experimentation, benchmarking, and regression testing without privacy review overhead or data handling restrictions that would otherwise slow down iteration. The privacy design is not a constraint on the system. It is what makes broad adoption possible.

Results and impact

Since starting this project, we have observed significant improvements across multiple dimensions.

On synthetic data quality, our internal scoring system showed significant quality gains in the structural, contextual, and statistical fidelity of the generated data. Across our composite quality metric (which measures how closely synthetic data mirrors the complexity and patterns of real enterprise environments), scores improved 39% compared to our initial generation approach. Some industry-specific environments reached quality scores above 0.9 out of 1.0, demonstrating that domain focused generation produces highly realistic evaluation environments. The improvements were obtained in part by incorporating realistic, industry signals and in part by automating quality improvements via key composite quality metrics that help improve the structural integrity, contextual coherence and statistical diversity of our synthetic industry environments.

On scale and efficiency, each synthetic environment now contains hundreds of users with complete communication histories across three industry verticals. Evaluation dataset creation has gone from multi-day manual effort to automated pipeline runs.

On organizational adoption, our industry evaluation data generation platforms have been published to an internal shared catalog for cross-team reuse and established as the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot. The difference wasn’t just incremental. It was a shift in how teams approach evaluation: from ad hoc, manual processes to standardized, reproducible infrastructure.

Conclusion

As we continue to expand what Microsoft Copilot can do, from single turn Q&A to agentic multi-step workflows, our commitment to evaluation remains at the heart of our approach. In enterprise AI, quality isn’t just about accuracy or speed. It’s about trust. Organizations need confidence that AI systems handle their information correctly, and that confidence can only come from thorough, repeatable evaluation. That trust rests on two commitments woven through everything we build: rigorous privacy protection and proactive content safety.

Looking ahead, Microsoft Copilot is tackling even more exciting evaluation challenges: How do we assess the quality of multi-turn agentic interactions? How do we extend synthetic environments to capture organizational dynamics evolving over months or years? How do we build evaluation frameworks for AI systems that take actions, not just generate text? These are the kinds of questions our team is working on next.

At Microsoft, we’re not just building AI. We’re building the infrastructure to ensure it works reliably for every enterprise, in every industry, at every scale.

Thanks to everyone who’s worked on Industry Evaluation Datasets!

More and more, AI agents are handling tasks that are complex.

[MUSIC FADES]

Tasks that require multiple steps, decisions, and interactions with external tools. But how can we count on AI agents to do the work if their ability to adjust when things go wrong may require a lot of resources with no guarantees of a better result?

A new self-improving framework called ForkPilot learns when it’s worth revisiting earlier decisions to find a different approach and adapts its strategy based on new outcomes.

Tested across six benchmarks and leading AI models, ForkPilot measures up to the best existing methods while reducing AI processing demands by up to 59%. These results suggest that AI agents can solve complex problems more reliably and efficiently, making them more practical and cost-effective to deploy at scale.

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

Understanding coding agent success and failure

Coding agents execute user queries by reasoning about, editing, and running code. Understanding why these agents fail is critical if we want to build more capable and reliable coding agents. Unfortunately, existing benchmarks often make it difficult to identify which factors contribute to success or failure.

CABRA is a framework for generating coding challenges from scratch. It lets researchers increase complexity in a controlled way and pinpoints the skills that are most difficult for agents.

Across thousands of generated challenges, the researchers found that agents often overcame coding problems by using tools. Yet the agents still struggled when they needed to understand unfamiliar codebases. The findings suggest that understanding existing code, rather than modifying it, remains one of the biggest obstacles to developing more effective coding agents.

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

Evolving agent skills with activity logs

Computer-use agents are AI systems that are designed to complete tasks that require clicking and typing. They can fill in forms, process requests, and navigate websites. To do this effectively, they need to learn the procedures that people use to get work done. User activity logs can offer a way to capture this knowledge. But activity logs typically don’t record the intent behind each action and often combine tasks.

The new framework TeleTune learns reusable skills and workflows from these logs. It also infers the task goals associated with the sequences of actions.

In evaluations across software and browser tasks, TeleTune outperformed existing approaches. By learning from existing activity, TeleTune offers a scalable way to help AI agents adapt to unfamiliar software and carry out complex, multi-step workflows

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

Looking beyond similarities in AI use (opens in new tab)

Workers across industries may appear to be using AI in surprisingly similar ways, but a closer look reveals a different story.

Microsoft researchers analyzed aggregated Copilot Chat activity across a broad range of customer categories and found that editing documents led all classified activities, accounting for more than 20 percent.

But when researchers set aside the 20 most common activities, differences between customer categories became substantially more pronounced. The most common uses of AI may be hiding important differences in how organizations use it for more specialized work.

For business leaders, the takeaway is clear: don’t assume you have the same AI needs as others in your industry. Finding the right opportunities means looking beyond usage statistics to understand what employees actually do, how they work, and what outcomes matter most.

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

Helping teachers make more time for teaching

A new study shows how Shiksha Copilot—a human-in-the-loop AI tool—could transform teacher workflows in Global South classrooms.

The study in low-resource schools in India found the tool reduced the time teachers spent on bilingual lesson planning and bureaucracy. That gave them more time to craft more engaging classroom activities.

More than a thousand teachers participated, and many reported reduced stress levels and a positive impression of how AI can help them. These teachers actively engaged with Shiksha Copilot, using their professional expertise to adapt and repurpose materials to suit their own classrooms.

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

Improving extended-range weather forecasting 

Ten-day weather forecasts have become remarkably dependable. But what about the weeks that follow?

The two-to-six-week window remains a major challenge for forecasting models, which is a problem. That’s when a wide range of critical decisions get made related to farming, managing wildfires, and preparing for extreme weather.

A new machine-learning framework called Probabilistic Bias Correction, or PBC, is helping close that gap. PBC learns from a weather model’s past mistakes and helps correct them.

And the early results are promising.

PBC took top honors in a global competition focused on improving extended-range forecasting. It’s also being deployed in Kenya, where it’s helping improve critical monsoon forecasts for farmers.

This development could help make weather predictions more useful across a broad range of applications.

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

BioEmu2 now available in public preview (opens in new tab)

BioEmu2, a new foundation model for understanding biomolecular structure, dynamics, and function, is now available in public preview.

Developed by the Microsoft Research AI for Science team, BioEmu2 builds on Biomolecular Emulator, a deep-learning model designed to help scientists better understand how proteins work.

That understanding could have important implications for medicine. By learning more about how proteins function, scientists could move closer to developing more effective medications that enhance beneficial protein activity or prevent proteins from causing harm.

Go to the BioEmu2 Microsoft Research GitHub repository (opens in new tab) to explore the model and learn more.

[MUSIC]

And that’s your Research Focus.

From more capable AI agents to better weather forecasting, these are just a few of the developments researchers are exploring at Microsoft.

Want to learn more and stay connected? Explore the latest research, discover the people behind it, and keep tabs on the ideas shaping what’s next by following Microsoft Research on major social platforms.

I’m Sowbhagya Suresh. Thanks so much for tuning in. We’ll see you in the next Microsoft Research Focus.

item.title: Flint-interactive: A language for creating interactive data visualizations
item.dc:creator: Chenglong Wang, Yuwei Xiao, Alper Sarikaya, Michel Galley, Chris Quirk, Jianfeng Gao
item.description:
Flint-interactive gives AI agents a language for creating interactive visualizations. Click a chart, filter data, highlight related content, and explore beyond the view the author originally chose.

The post Flint-interactive: A language for creating interactive data visualizations appeared first on Microsoft Research.
item.content:encoded:
At a glance

  • Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions.
  • Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators.
  • Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations.
  • Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another.

AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports with data visualizations. They help users examine patterns more efficiently than by reading verbose text. However, when we’re feeling exploratory, we want to go beyond static visualizations.: We want to interact with charts to zoom in on details, compare data across charts, or even highlight related text in the document from a chart selection, and vice versa. This requires agents to be able to create interactive data visualizations that communicate information while letting readers explore beyond the author’s chosen view, ideally with the quality of interactive stories in sophisticated data journalism. This leaves us wondering: 

  • (As a user) Can I interact with charts directly in chat to explore the data and ask follow-up questions based on what I select?
  • (As a developer) Can I enable the AI agents I build for my customers to generate interactive visualizations that help them explore and understand their data?

Yes, it’s possible, but there is a significant practical gap. Even with capable frontier models, we still face:

  • High generation cost. Agents rarely produce a fully satisfactory interactive visualization in one turn. Repeated rounds of reasoning, coding, and debugging consume tokens and time.
  • Reliability. Interactive visualizations are challenging enough that expressive interactive charts introduce poor layouts or broken interactions easily, and we risk introducing new problems when trying to fix them.

These challenges help explain why consistently generating high-quality interactive visualizations remain difficult in real-world use. Meanwhile, built-in interactions in some visualization libraries are not expressive enough on their own to create bespoke interactive charts. And these challenges are results of the lack of an expressive yet high-level language to specify visual interactions.

PODCAST SERIES

The AI Revolution in Medicine, Revisited

Join Microsoft’s Peter Lee on a journey to discover how AI is impacting healthcare and what it means for the future of medicine.

Listen now
Opens in a new tab

Flint-interactive

Flint-interactive (opens in new tab) is a language for creating interactive data visualizations on top of Flint. It allows users to create dashboards, data stories, and interactive artifacts more easily. The power of Flint-interactive comes from Flint’s compiler, which translates user interactions into semantic events that capture the meaning behind what users select. It then uses high-level operators to update visualizations in response to those events, making sophisticated interactions far easier to create and maintain. This shifts the heavy burden of resolving complex dependencies between interaction and visual logic to the compiler, so the user (or the agent) can easily describe expressive interactions with high-level specifications.

How to use

1. Use Flint in your chat

Use Flint Interactive directly in your chat or canvas environment through Flint-MCP and MCP Apps, following the MCP setup guide. With the latest release, tell your agent what to chart and which interactions you want; it can generate an interaction_spec alongside the Flint chart spec and render the interactive chart in your conversation.

2. Build an interactive app with Flint

Build interactive charts in a dashboard, data story, or other application with Flint Interactive Canvas. Your app can use event handlers to process semantic events emitted by Flint Canvas, for example to filter a table, update another chart, or change application state. To let your app’s widgets control how the chart updates, send update operators to Flint Canvas.

3. Create bespoke interactions

To create bespoke interactions beyond Flint’s presets, define a trigger and a custom handle function with the programming API that maps semantic events to custom chart update sequences. For example, a handler can highlight a clicked country and label it by name. It combines set-style and set-annotation without manipulating renderer-specific marks.

How it works

Flint Canvas is a state machine that tracks user interactions on the canvas and manages visual rendering state. Flint makes interaction specification easy by separating visual logic, managed by the compiler, from interaction logic, specified by the user at the semantic level:

  • Visual logic: The compiler automatically resolves raw triggers, such as clicks, drags, and key presses, into semantic events that identify chart elements and data. It also translates update operators into rendered canvas changes, handling hit testing, and low-level visual updates.
  • Interaction logic: The user specifies interactions by mapping semantic interaction events to chart update operators, such as set style to highlight data, set annotation to label a point, or set viewport to pan or zoom. The user can also use those semantic events to update external tables, widgets, or application states. 

This separation means users do not need to reverse-engineer rendering logic or manipulate renderer-specific marks, making interactions easier to specify and maintain. Furthermore, because event generation and visual updates are compositional, the same model also connects Flint with tables, text, other charts, and widgets to build interactive stories and dashboards.

Try it now!

Chart users: Set up Flint in your chat (opens in new tab) and ask your agent to create an interactive chart. Find inspiration in the interaction gallery.

App builders: Build interactive dashboards, data stories, and connected views with the programming API (opens in new tab). Share the interaction-author skill with your coding agent to add presets to your app.

Interaction designers: Explore the bespoke examples (opens in new tab), design a new interaction, and turn it into a reusable preset. Propose a preset on GitHub and share your prototype or implementation to help expand Flint’s interaction vocabulary.

item.dc:creator: Xinzhi Zhang
item.description:

item.content:encoded:
Microsoft researcher and collaborator combine new mathematical ideas with human-directed AI to resolve a central problem in high-dimensional geometry and probability

At a glance

  • Fundamental scientific breakthrough: Researchers resolved the Kannan-Lovász-Simonovits (KLS) conjecture, a 31-year-old problem widely regarded as one of the central open questions in high-dimensional geometry, with implications for statistics, optimization, algorithms, and computer science.
  • A universal geometric principle: The result establishes a universal geometric principle for log-concave distributions, showing that simple flat cuts can capture their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension. 
  • Human-AI collaboration: The breakthrough emerged from a human-directed agentic research process in which AI systems explored mathematical possibilities while researchers evaluated, pruned, and redirected the search.
  • Independent confirmation: Multiple independent researchers have validated this research, identifying its central criterion as the key breakthrough, followed by a machine-checked formal verification. 

For decades, a fundamental question about the difficulty of computing in high-dimensional spaces has resisted proof. New research resolves this question, removing a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing.

The Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits (KLS) conjecture was proposed in 1995. It asks whether, for a broad class of high-dimensional probability distributions, the best flat or hyperplane cut is always nearly as effective as the best cut of any shape. More precisely, KLS predicts that the two differ by no more than a universal constant, regardless of the number of dimensions. This would establish a dimension-free geometric principle with important consequences for high-dimensional geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. Because the geometry of these cuts governs how quickly random walks can explore a distribution, KLS also plays a central role in the theory of high-dimensional sampling.

Since 1995, mathematicians have accumulated evidence that the conjecture was true, but a complete proof remained elusive. Now, two researchers, including Xinzhi Zhang from the Machine Learning and Optimization group at Microsoft Research, have proved the KLS conjecture (opens in new tab). They have shown that the relationship holds with a fixed bound, regardless of how many dimensions a shape has. Before this work, the best known result (opens in new tab), established in July 2026, allowed that bound to grow slowly as the number of dimensions increased. This work establishes a fundamental geometric principle: high-dimensional spaces are better behaved than previously known, and the obstacles to navigating them do not grow without bound as dimensions increase. 

The importance of the KLS conjecture was recognized across the field long before it was resolved. In its 2017-18 Annual Report, the Mathematical Sciences Research Institute (MSRI) (opens in new tab) called it “a central open problem in high-dimensional convex geometry.” The Simons Institute (opens in new tab) described it as “one of the most important open problems in convex geometry.” In the proceedings of the 2022 International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) (opens in new tab), Ronen Eldan noted its broad implications for high-dimensional convex and computational geometry. Quanta Magazine (opens in new tab) wrote that KLS “lies at the heart of many questions in statistics and computer science.”

Technical details

The authors began by improving the July 2026 result in order to make the mathematical bound more precise. Working with AI agents in a structured, human-directed process, they explored more than 100 candidate approaches, many involving lengthy calculations with higher-order tensors. This produced a new mathematical criterion that became the foundation of the final proof.

The authors then discovered that the new criterion could be applied recursively. Each improved bound could be fed back into the same argument to produce a still tighter one. In the October 1, 2026 version of the paper, this reduced the dependence on dimension to the iterated logarithm. This function grows extraordinarily slowly, but it still grows with the dimension and therefore did not yet fully resolve the conjecture.

The final step was to repeat the entire recursive refinement, rather than applying it only once. This idea was inspired by the authors’ earlier work on fast algorithms for linear programming. The authors proved that the small errors introduced at each stage shrink fast enough that their total remains bounded by a universal constant, independent of the dimension. This eliminated the dependence on the number of dimensions and completed the proof in the October 4, 2026 version of the paper.

The recursive method, its repeated application, and the proof that the accumulated errors remain bounded are original contributions of the researchers. AI tools helped explore candidate approaches, carry out detailed derivations, prepare the manuscript, and perform internal proof checks. The researchers determined the mathematical direction, selected the promising ideas, assembled them into the final argument, and verified the proof.

Independent confirmation

On the same day that the authors posted their complete proof, a separate group of leading experts posted a full proof (opens in new tab) that they developed in parallel. Their work built upon the findings in the first version (opens in new tab) of the Microsoft paper, calling it “the crucial step in the proof.” A third proof (opens in new tab) which appeared separately on the same day relies on a closely related idea. In addition, a Lean 4 formalization (opens in new tab) was subsequently released, combining the key criterion from the first Microsoft paper with additional research. 

Independent proofs are among mathematics’ strongest forms of validation because they demonstrate that a result does not rest on a single chain of reasoning. The subsequent appearance of alternative approaches and formal verification further strengthens confidence that the field has uncovered a genuine underlying principle rather than a fragile technical argument. The authors have also shortened their proof and verified the streamlined argument in Lean; they plan to release both after final review. Together, these developments provide complementary forms of confirmation.

Human-AI guidance

In the process of proving KLS, this research also demonstrates the power of having researchers direct AI rather than simply asking AI to solve a complex problem through a single end-to-end run of a frontier model or agent. The authors used an agentic search process with iterative, human-assisted “pruning”: As multiple agents explored variations of an idea in parallel, the researcher examined their intermediate result, eliminated unpromising directions, and passed the most promising result to the next round. Roughly one hundred research trajectories were explored before the key breakthrough emerged. 

In a separate track of the project, the authors made repeated unguided attempts to solve the same problem with several leading AI models, using roughly the same total token budget as the main process. That effort fell short of the goal. The eventual success depended on both the capabilities of the AI systems and the mathematical judgment of the researchers. 

Conclusion

Taken together, resolving KLS settles a central problem in high-dimensional geometry. A wide range of results that previously relied on the conjecture as an assumption can now be stated unconditionally. The proof therefore provides a stronger foundation for research in convex geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science.

The work also demonstrates how carefully guided human-AI collaboration can contribute to genuine scientific discovery while reinforcing, rather than replacing human insight. It highlights the continuing importance of scientific judgment in identifying promising directions, recognizing conceptual connections, and seeing when a partial insight points toward a deeper result. The authors are now simplifying the proof and extending its formal verification so that the mathematics and theoretical computer science communities can more easily examine the result and build on it.

Acknowledgements 

Thank you to our co-author Zhao Song for his contributions to this work, and Victor Reis (opens in new tab) and Ishai Menache for helpful discussions throughout the project.

item.title: Called to serve: Tech, research, and positive impact
item.dc:creator: Weishung Liu, Chris White
item.description:
Lab Director Chris White has worked on research challenges with real-world implications—from new approaches to wartime data analysis to tools for combating human trafficking. He talks to program manager Weishung Liu about the influences that led to the work and more.

The post Called to serve: Tech, research, and positive impact appeared first on Microsoft Research.
item.content:encoded:
In the summer of 2010, postdoc Chris White worked with a multidisciplinary team at the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, or DARPA, to determine if a new approach to data analysis could prevent violence and protect troops during the war in Afghanistan. At the conclusion of the program, the agency asked White to prove the value of his work—on the ground. 

In this episode, Principal Technical Program Manager Weishung Liu talks with White, director of Catalyst Lab at Microsoft Research, about his unexpected break from academic research to help lead advanced tech operations in Afghanistan and his later decision to again work on tech with immediate, real-world implications: dark-web search tools used to help combat human trafficking. Liu and White explore the influences that led to these experiences plus the important role of problem selection in innovation and remaining hopeful after seeing the darkest parts of humanity. 

Subscribe to the Microsoft Research Podcast:

  • Apple Podcasts
  • Email
  • Android
  • Spotify
  • RSS Feed

Transcript 

[MUSIC] 

CHRIS WHITE: I have seen a lot of really bad humanity. You know, I’ve seen terrorism and trafficking and sophisticated organized crime, you know, designed to take things from people. Designed to hurt people. And I just know that I can do something about it, you know, and that I have and that we can. And so I think that that light, you know, the light of making a difference, you know, allows me to hold and handle, you know, the dark parts. 

[THEME MUSIC] 

STANDARD INTRODUCTION: This is the Microsoft Research Podcast, where Microsoft researchers—driving advancement through fundamental science and technology research—explore the who, how, and what’s next in computing and AI. 

[MUSIC ENDS] 

WEISHUNG LIU: Hi, and welcome. I’m Weishung Liu, a principal technical program manager here at Microsoft Research, and today I’m talking to Dr. Christopher White, who leads Microsoft Research’s Catalyst Lab. 

Chris has one of those careers that sounds almost made up: a Harvard postdoc, on-the-ground advanced tech lead during the war in Afghanistan, a DARPA program manager, a dark web search pioneer, and a public-good technologist. And his work has been featured in Popular Science (opens in new tab) as well as recognized with honors, including the 2016 Presidential Award for Extraordinary Efforts to Combat Trafficking in Persons (opens in new tab). 

But what I’m most interested in today is the person behind that résumé. How someone who has seen some of the worst as part of his work still comes to the office with a smile and a commitment to building tools that make the world better. 

Chris, thanks for joining me. 

WHITE: Thanks for having me, Wei. Nice to see you. 

LIU: Yeah, good to see you, too. And so let’s get started. So I’ve known you for, I think, maybe around five or maybe six years, and now I work with you in Catalyst Lab. I love your story, and when I tell people about you, I say that you lead the newly formed Cat Lab, or Catalyst Lab, in Microsoft Research, you were a senior executive at DARPA, and you are married to an incredibly accomplished woman and scholar. And I personally think that your life story would make a very watchable Hollywood film. So when you tell your own story, though, where do you start? 

WHITE: Well, you start from where you are. And where I am today is leading research at Microsoft during a period of great fear and hope about changing technology and society. 

LIU: But, like, that’s now. There’s clearly lots of time from now into before, you know, the before times. So, like, tell me a little bit about the before times. Like, where were you at—I think you grew up in Oklahoma maybe. Tell me about that. Tell me about Chris White, the child. 

WHITE: Well, I was nerdy. I was a nerdy Eagle Scout. [LAUGHTER] I liked to build my own computers and have local area network [LAN] parties with my friends. But I also really liked being outside. I liked being in nature and camping and rock climbing. Those were all important to me. 

LIU: OK, you mentioned LAN parties. Tell me about … what did we play with our friends? 

WHITE: Well, you know, we played everything. I preferred playing sports games, but I lost a lot of the other ones. 

LIU: [LAUGHS] Wait, so you played like LAN party sports games, like, in basements? Like, with your … were we all in the same … ? 

WHITE: Yeah. Attics. It was attics. Yeah, not basements. [LAUGHTER] Mm-hmm. Yeah. Everybody had to bring their own computer or bring their own Ethernet cable. And the more that you had your own machine that was higher powered, the better you were going to play. 

LIU: So did you have the best machine? 

WHITE: I had the best machine. I built the best machine. Until someone built a better machine. But it was the best for a while. 

And I had a budget for it. And my family didn’t understand that the budget also included two giant speakers, like the size of a computer tower, like subwoofer speakers. They didn’t know that was part of the computer building process. But it turns out that excellent audio-visual is a critical part of a well-functioning machine. 

LIU: I love it. But, OK, we’re going to focus a little bit … continue focusing on childhood. So you mentioned nerdy kid, which means—I’m going to generalize here—debate team or math competition team or chess team? 

WHITE: Oh, it was the debate team. Yeah. Debate was a really wonderful activity. It taught me how to understand many sides of an issue and taught me how to think about evidence and research in that way. 

LIU: So, Chris, take me back again. Like, we’re talking a little bit about Oklahoma, and, you know, at some point, you chose researcher. Like, I—for example—when I was a kid, I was convinced I would be an architect. I am not an architect as you can see. But did you always think you were going to be a researcher? Was there an epiphany there? Like … or was it always kind of like a slow hunch that you were going to pursue research as a career? 

WHITE: Yeah, I kind of always felt like it. You know, as I was applying for school, those were the kinds of jobs I was interested in. You know, the kinds of things that you do, you know, once you finish degrees that have research in them. Those were the people, when I visited their work, I was inspired by. The people that were discovering, you know, that were inventing, that were innovating, that were … they’re pushing the boundaries that were kind of in that unknown, you know, space and making sense of it. 

And so I’ve always had that curiosity, you know, and that approach to discovery. And so as I increased my education, it just changed the nature of what research meant and the ways in which I imagined that process evolving. 

LIU: Was a doctorate always on the cards then? Or did that come, like, as you were in college and then gradually learned and thought, you know, I could keep going? 

WHITE: Yeah, you know, I didn’t know about doctorates really when I went to college. I wasn’t as familiar with higher education. And so I knew that I wanted, you know, advanced degrees. And I knew that I wanted more than was being taught in the undergraduate level. But I didn’t know, you know, for example, that when you apply to PhD programs, that often you get paid to go. You know, you get admitted and you get a stipend. 

You know, I was familiar with law and medicine and that you take out loans and you have to do it this way. And so for me, it was a surprise to know that I could apply to PhD programs directly from college. And from then, I just really was excited, you know, that I could explore different universities and different areas of focus and build on, you know, strong technical foundations of math and science and physics. 

And it was really amazing mentors that helped me and opened doors and inspired me. You know, mentors at Oklahoma State University, Johns Hopkins, and Harvard, really people that took their time and helped me. I’m really grateful for my teachers. 

LIU: So let’s talk about your first mentor of your life, and I’m going to assume … Dad? 

WHITE: Yeah, Dad’s a big influence. 

LIU: OK, Dad’s a big influence. And so we’re going to, I’m going to go down this path. So Catalyst Lab landed a huge commitment from our executive, kind of, leadership team on a project that has been, I think, like a decade in the making. And then … so we all, I know we all came together on a call. We’re like, “Wow, let’s debrief. Let’s talk about it.” Like, oh, energy’s up. And then at the very end of the meeting, you said, “OK, now I’m going to go clean some toilets.” 

WHITE: [LAUGHS] Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. 

LIU: And I think all of us kind of thought, like, wha-what does that mean? So before we get kind of more into the specifics of mentorship and the, like, follow-on in your career, what— please tell me—does cleaning toilets have to do with success? 

WHITE: Well, you know, like I said, Dad’s a big influence, and he taught me so many things, and he taught me about respecting people. And most importantly, he taught me about humility and service. And so his way of making sure I understood that was every time something really good happened to me, he’d remind me to go clean some toilets and, sort of, embody that. And so I did. I did it last weekend actually. I went to a community event and volunteered to do bathroom clean. 

LIU: Is this like … are you … so in, like, the household chores, are you, like, the bathroom cleaner? Like, is this just always your job when we’re dividing up chores in the house? 

WHITE: No, no, no. We trade off, and also we have a complicated household, and so we have a lot of help that also helps with cleaning. And so this is something that I choose to do, especially if I can do it in a community context, because it again reminds me, you know, about humility and about service and of respect for other people and other jobs. 

LIU: So I think this … there’s some Eagle Scout vibes that I’m getting from here, as well, based on sort of humility and service. What is the Boy Scout badge you are most proud of? 

WHITE: Oh, that’s really hard. Each badge is something that you earn, including the Eagle Scout badge. And the Eagle Scout badge for me was maybe the most difficult to earn because it requires an Eagle project. And I was really close to my Eagle project. I was, I was … had it set up and it was ready to go. And it was in this church in downtown Oklahoma City in 1995. And right as I was about to do this project, the Murrah Building blew up in a terrorist incident (opens in new tab), … 

LIU: Whoa. 

WHITE: … and it blew up part of the church. And, therefore, my Eagle project was not realistic, and it was not a priority, and it got shelved. And it took me several years after that to then come back to plan and execute an ambitious Eagle project right before I turned 18. And so that badge, … 

LIU: Wow. 

WHITE: … you know, completing the project, overcoming significant setbacks, including being a teenager and having other interests, to come through and finish it, I’m really proud of finishing it. 

LIU: That’s awesome. So you … so that was, so there were a few years then in between when you ideated, had the idea for the project, and then … I appreciate the story around resilience because of when you completed the project. Like, what is the biggest takeaway that you took from there? Like what is that big lesson? You turned 18, you finished it, you celebrate. Actually, you know, maybe I’ll ask you, how did you celebrate? 

WHITE: Oh, with my family. You know, the Boy Scouts is a long process. It’s many years, many kinds of roles, many kinds of learning, and to finish it—I finished it with another of my fellow scouts that had been together for a long time. And so our families, we had a ceremony, and it was something we could celebrate. And every time I think about it, I think about the things that you keep repeating when you attend the scout things, like the motto, “being prepared,” and the, kind of, laws about being respectful and courteous. And those are things that continue to be, you know, principles that influence my priorities and also inspire me and help me in my job. 

LIU: Before we get to your job then, we’re going to talk about this interim period where I’ll just say you chose to go to war and a few other things in between. Let’s jump to 2010, when you joined DARPA, which is the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, within the Department of War. And then, I think, very quickly afterwards you were sent to Afghanistan to help implement a new approach to wartime analysis. And then … but before that, I think you were a Harvard postdoc, and you had actually mentioned it was a mentor who encouraged you to attend a meeting with DARPA that resulted in this course change. 

And so now I’m super curious, how did this conversation happen where you were, you know, promising Harvard postdoc, which became a mentor going, “Hey, there’s something happening. You should go attend.” Like, what happened there? 

WHITE: Yeah. DARPA invests taxpayer money, and they have a record of really creating innovations, massive innovations (opens in new tab). You know, the internet, GPS, stealth, UAVs. And at the time, there was different ways of building programs, and one of the kind of tested ways was to bring together different fields of expertise. 

And so we were in wartime in Afghanistan. DARPA was not involved very much. And there was a question: you know, could we bring together social scientists with math people, computer science and defense experts, and together could they help us make sense of what’s happening in the data? Could that be useful to prevent violence and to protect our soldiers? And it was an experiment because it required all these different areas of expertise coming together—from sensors through analysis through social behavior—and a culture change. And so the summer was a Skunk Works to understand, was there something to contribute? 

And at the end of it, they asked me, they said, “Well, you know, do you believe in your work?” And I was like, “Yeah.” You know, like, “Well, do you … can you prove it? You know, can you go see if it can help protect our soldiers and help prevent violence?” And so they asked me to be of service, and I said yeah. 

And it was something that I was really unprepared for. I was supposed to go for nine days the first time, and on the third day, I got a battlefield promotion and was put in charge and then ended up staying for 90 days and then went back a few times after that even. And so, you know, our work was towards … oriented towards protecting, you know, soldiers and toward preventing violence and using AI and advanced technology to do that. And it was a, really, a big opportunity. 

LIU: So you attended a meeting, you contributed some work, and then, you know, “Do you believe in your work? Prove it.” What was the time frame between, you know, like, showing up at meeting, participating in some of the research before, like, “prove it”? Was it years, or was it months? 

WHITE: The … no, no, the … so the Skunk Works was a summer. It was like, you know, 40 days of, kind of, like focused effort. But at the end of it, I was expecting to go back to Harvard and continue my postdoc. But instead, you know, they sat us down; they said, “Look, you know, we think this can make a difference. You know, do you think so?” And when I said yeah, from then to getting over there was like a week. It was an extremely fast … 

LIU: What? 

WHITE: … turnaround. It was extremely urgent and, you know, unexpected. 

LIU: OK, so, like, how … so you said, yes, like I believe in my work. They gave you … they essentially said, OK, then go next week. And how, how does somebody prepare for an experience like that? If you can even prepare. 

WHITE: Yeah, I don’t know. You know, this was an experiment. You know, sending researchers—even having a presence from DARPA—in the war zone, (opens in new tab) it was new. And the idea was there could be a difference made because technology was advancing quickly. And that meant that many of the mechanisms in place for other ways of getting prepared were not available. And there was a bunch of training, like crash courses in training on what to do in certain situations, how things work, you know, how to handle yourself in different ways. But it was … it was very brief. 

And so there wasn’t a lot of preparation because also we were planning to be there for nine days. But because there was an opportunity to do something good, that extended, and there was a lot of learning on the job and a lot of support in theater, a lot of people really willing to help us because we were helping them. 

LIU: So, OK, so you talked about lots of people there, lots of people supporting. I’m not going to focus too much on your time in Afghanistan because that was covered really well in a Popular Science article. But I do have to ask, can you tell me the origin story of the nickname Dr. Spaghetti Man? 

WHITE: [LAUGHS] Sure. Sure. You know, I’m a long-time yoga practitioner. You know, 20-plus years. It’s how I keep myself calibrated. And in Kabul, I was practicing yoga in the gym, and all these people were staring at me. You know, they were staring at me before their … they had a class; they had, like, a combatives class, a kind of different judo-mixed-martial-arts class. 

And, you know, I had a little bit of training, and so after a couple of times, I decided I’d just join in. And I joined in, and I won a lot. I won a lot of the matches. And one of the matches I won, turns out, it was against the Marine who was guarding the entrance to the building I was working in across the headquarters. And he told everyone. He told everyone, you know, that this, like, lanky spaghetti guy, you know, like, got out of things and beat him, and he did it in such a way that everyone in the building knew. And so I got all this respect, and I got that cool nickname. 

LIU: Did other folks challenge you as a result of this Marine telling your story? 

WHITE: I mean, everyone that came to that class was game, you know. And I didn’t, you know, I couldn’t beat everybody, but I held my own, and that was really surprising to a lot of people. And again, once you establish yourself in different ways, you know, there is a lot of respect and, um, camaraderie. 

LIU: So, you know, tell me, what did that whole experience teach you about, like, a life lived, and how do those lessons show up in your work today, including the, you know, Spaghetti Man experience? 

WHITE: You know, the whole thing, it taught me about, you know, service and what it means to serve, and it taught me about the reality of both peace and violence in the world. And that continued to motivate me to make a difference. 

LIU: After your time in Afghanistan, you continued on with DARPA as a program manager, and in that role, you developed Memex (opens in new tab), which I believe is a set of tools that could be mixed and matched to help uncover some really shady and dark parts of the web, which from what I understand was really hard to do up until that point. 

I think this work also is what helped you … what you received your 2016 presidential award on. And, you know, like, can you … how do you explain the Memex project and this dark web work to someone outside tech? And what about this project inspired or appealed to you to even pursue it? 

WHITE: Yeah, well, the inspiration started when I was overseas because I saw the benefit of evidence when it came to stopping bad things from happening and prosecuting them. And coming back to the US, I saw more and more opportunities where collecting evidence at large scale was a really useful mechanism. And so, you know, people think of search engines a lot, and search engines are a great tool for finding something, but when you need to connect the dots, there wasn’t a great tool that could work at the scale of the web and connect the dots, especially some of the dots being in difficult places that were not very visible. 

And so by creating a technology that would connect the dots across parts of the internet (opens in new tab), it allowed the prosecution of these kinds of really awful [trafficking] crimes, and so for example, in New York City, it allowed them to increase their prosecutions by 10 times because it gave them new evidence and different kinds of evidence than they had before, and they could use that in a way to really deal with the issue differently. 

LIU: OK, from what I understand, the dark web is a pretty—ha-ha—dark place, [LAUGHS] and so, like, you’ve worked in some very dark spaces and close to some very dark uses of the technology. So, like, how again, like, you and I interact a lot, and so it’s always curious to me, how has that not made you cynical and how do you stay hopeful? 

WHITE: You know, I think what it’s done is it’s really increased my motivation. You know, my motivation to make a contribution. You know, my motivation to stay aware and be realistic. And by being realistic and motivated to address some of these very challenging issues, you know, around violence, around harm, and instead to focus on empowerment and to focus on justice, it gave me something to do. 

And so I have seen a lot of really bad humanity, you know. I’ve seen terrorism and trafficking and sophisticated organized crime, you know, designed to take things from people. Designed to hurt people. And I just know that I can do something about it, you know, and that I have and that we can. And so it’s really been inspiring to, you know, for example, come to Microsoft, where there is a mission of empowerment and there is that perspective that technology can make a difference. And so I think that light, you know, the light of making a difference, you know, allows me to hold and handle, you know, the dark parts. 

LIU: I mean, that’s a very powerful message, right? Because even with the darkest parts of humanity, there is light, or, you know, you cannot have darkness without light, as well. 

I think there may have been a 60 Minutes interview (opens in new tab) that included a short snippet of you talking about your work, and you had shared with me that—which, by the way, I cannot find the 60 Minutes episode, and I desperately want to. But, you know, I heard perhaps through you, Chris, that that 60 Minutes episode actually contributed to you coming to Microsoft maybe or, you know, getting a job at Microsoft, and that made me curious. Like, after some really incredible experiences, after all of that, why did you choose Microsoft? 

WHITE: Oh, it was a … it was a really good choice. And at the time, I had a lot of options, and I was looking around, and this mix of the mission of the company—this mission of empowering everyone—and the scope of the company, you know, being, you know, IT for the world, you know, platforms and infrastructure for the world, and my confidence in its leader. You know, the CEO was part of my interview process. And, you know, that together gave me, you know, this perspective that I could do something here. You know, that there … I could start to envision moving from, you know, for example, very high-powered, expensive lasers to table knives. They both cut, and the world needs both of them. 

LIU: One of the things that you talk a lot about is problem selection. And I think sometimes that also gets referred to as taste these days. So how do you think about problem selection in Microsoft Research, in Catalyst Lab, given the breadth of what Microsoft does? 

WHITE: Oh, I think it’s just the most important part of research. You know, it’s the place where the angle of the whole thing changes, and it allows you to start to imagine a different future, you know, or to work backward from that future that you want to see and see what you can do to contribute to it now. And the amazing thing about Microsoft Research is there’s tremendous freedom, and so there’s tremendous creativity in problem selection. 

And it’s the kind of thing where you have that latitude to go from idea to evidence to this potential for growth and thriving and along the way get feedback about value and usability and benefit or policy or adaptability, integration. And so its scope provides so many vehicles for growth and utility of advanced research ideas. 

And its mission, you know, allows the focus of those to address absolutely critical problems. You know, problems of, you know, impending security challenges due to AI, problems of advanced, you know, memory and storage; it allows for, you know, personalization automation, just, you know, for example. And I think that this mix of freedom combined with responsibility and mechanisms, you know, to prove out and demonstrate value, that that combination is just really remarkable and it really motivates me to take the opportunity seriously. 

LIU: So it’s almost going to be like asking you about your favorite kids now. What are some, what are some accomplishments in Microsoft Research or Catalyst Lab that you are particularly proud of? 

WHITE: Oh, you know, I think that, you know, right now, for example—again, focusing on kind of where we are—I think that we have a real opportunity to contribute something in the cyber defense space. I think our work on security and AI and hacking, it’s really in, you know, based on such a deep expertise and also based on, you know, people with a lot of experience, and I think it’s growing in need, you know, the need to protect our digital infrastructure, the need to deter and interdict people that would like to break systems or cause harm, that’s really growing right now. And so being able to show up in a way that creates breakthrough that can scale with relevance to address that growing need, it’s really something that’s, you know, awesome to me. 

And also I think that again kind of extending from the, sort of, Memex conversation, where we’re trying to connect the dots, you know, these days, trying to analyze lots of content as part of being more efficient, as part of being more creative, as part of being more capable, you know, using tools to augment that human taste and creativity and ingenuity, that’s really never been as powerful as it is before and continues to grow. And so I think making contributions in these areas, you know, where we have state-of-the-art technology and we’re creating changes in the way systems are getting built and used, to me, it shows that, you know, despite the fast pace of change and despite the extreme competitiveness in the technology sector, that specialized expertise with good problem selection and an environment to grow and get feedback can create the kind of breakthroughs that matter. And so I really like that. 

Maybe to give one more example from the past––just maybe something emblematic of the group and some of my predecessors––was this underwater datacenter called Project Natick (opens in new tab), [LAUGHTER] where this experiment, you know, put a datacenter in a submersible on the bottom of the ocean connected to a wind farm, and it tested this design about, could you build something that didn’t require human intervention? Could it be more efficient with power? Could it be more efficient with heat? 

And the program manager that created that is one of the best I’ve ever worked with. And it just performed incredibly well as this huge surprise, and it led to us being, you know, named the most innovative company [World Changing Company of the Year] in 2021 (opens in new tab) and other awards (opens in new tab). And it’s just an example of really out-there thinking, imagining a world that had challenges with water access and power access and land but where we need, you know, computation and data storage and technical capability available. 

So a little bit out there, but I really … I feel like we have to be imagining these different futures. We have to be radical in that way so that we can start to work back and make contributions now. 

LIU: I love the Natick example because I feel like Natick is the gift that keeps on giving. And, you know, if I can digress for a minute, I remember that I think one of the first TikTok videos that the Microsoft account posted was of Natick (opens in new tab)[1], but it was using, like, a meme at the time which had, like, human eyes and a mouth being lowered into, uh, and it was of Natick being lowered into the ocean, including like a Clippy, like a real-life Clippy swimming across the … it was … I still love that video for reasons why I don’t understand. [LAUGHTER] But if you haven’t seen it, highly recommend. Maybe we can link it [LAUGHS] if the video still exists. 

WHITE: Definitely. Look, look, one of the highlights was the fish cam. 

LIU: Yes! 

WHITE: You know, people were concerned that it might disrupt the marine ecosystem. And we did a lot of preparation and study for that. And just to be sure, we put cameras and watched it happen. 

LIU: Yep. 

WHITE: And all these fish kept coming around and making it home. And there was, like, computer vision that was analyzing which fishes and their movement, and it became like an always-on thing that people would just tune in to online to watch the fish. 

LIU: There was a seal. There was a seal. There were a couple seals that came by, … 

WHITE: Yeah. 

LIU: … too, which, yeah, I remember that. That’s really cool. Thanks for sharing. 

WHITE: Yeah, so you have to go not just out of the box but out of the datacenter. 

LIU: [LAUGHS] Oh no. All right. All right. 

So, Chris, before letting you go, it would be a missed opportunity if I did not ask you to share some practical advice and reflections given the breadth of your experience and lessons that you learned. So I’m going to do … maybe it doesn’t have to be a super-fast lightning round, but it’s going to be a lightning round of a couple of questions. 

WHITE: Sure. 

LIU: All right. One, what is the advice that you have received in your life that blew your mind or changed your perspective? 

WHITE: You’ve got to look out for the right place and the right time with the right people because it takes all those things to come together for magic to happen and to make a difference. 

LIU: OK, I’m going to have to ask. This is not … I’m breaking my own lightning round. How do you know? Like, how do you know if it’s the right place or the right time or the right people? 

WHITE: The universe gives a lot of feedback. You know, it’s something that with good listening, you can hear. 

LIU: What did … what did the universe tell you? 

WHITE: Told me to marry my wife. 

LIU: [LAUGHS] Ohhhh. Good choice. Good universe. Good universe. OK, next. 

WHITE: Yeah. Told me to have my kids. Absolutely. 

LIU: All right, next. Lesson you learned the hard way or the misstep that humbled you? 

WHITE: I’ve got to slow down. My tendency is to push too fast and too hard, and that can really lead to problems. And slowing down, it doesn’t in the end slow everything down. It just actually makes it just right and just enough. 

LIU: What’s an example of slow down? 

WHITE: Well, you know, I think there’s slowing down in making decisions, especially about people, compared to other kinds of decisions. Or even in my yoga practice. Slowing down the way that I use my body so that it can be healthy and strong for a long time. 

LIU: I do believe that one of your … the advice that you often give us in Cat Lab is take a vacation. 

WHITE: Absolutely. 

LIU: So slow down definitely fits that. 

WHITE: Get some perspective. 

LIU: So next question: talent or accomplishment you’re most proud of if given the chance to brag. And you have stated humility many times, and I’m going to ask you to just turn that bit off for a little bit and brag a little bit instead. 

WHITE: Mm-hmm. Well, I think it would be putting my leg behind my head and saying [LAUGHTER] the alphabet backwards while playing a percussion instrument. 

LIU: Hold on. Like, this is for realsies, and this is, like, this is not an AI-generated statement … 

WHITE: No. 

LIU: … or prompt? This is … And you’ve done this before? 

WHITE: I have. I’ve done it in a leadership offsite. 

LIU: [LAUGHS] You did not. 

WHITE: I did. 

LIU: I am going to need to ask some of our colleagues about that particular experience, but there was a percussion instrument? 

WHITE: Yeah. There was. But, you know, all kidding aside, you know, the 2016 presidential medal, you know, being able to make such a difference in a way for so many people that were affected and to also change the way technology was used from the data collection evidence, you know, through judicial proceedings, that process and arc, you know, is definitely something I’m extremely proud of, was extremely difficult, and I would definitely go for it again. 

LIU: I love it. OK, I love asking this one. You know I’ve asked people this a lot. Career path you would have chosen if you did not become a researcher—and you’re not allowed to say yoga teacher. 

WHITE: [LAUGHS] No, I would just be a different kind of researcher. 

LIU: No! 

WHITE: Yeah, definitely. Yeah. 

LIU: Really? OK, so if not an AI or computer science researcher, what else would we be researching? 

WHITE: Oh, the brain. You know, the … 

LIU: OK, how about a non-STEM research topic? [LAUGHS] 

WHITE: Anthropology. 

LIU: OK, OK, fine. So, like, no, there’s no scenario where research is not in the picture. 

WHITE: No, it just seems to be part of me, you know, part of my drive, you know, part of what gives me energy, keeps me motivated and curious. And this, you know, frontier, it allows that evolution to keep unfolding. 

LIU: OK. All right. Good to know. So not yoga teacher. Always some form of research. 

WHITE: Well, I mean, yoga teacher is a kind of researcher into the universe. 

LIU: What?! [LAUGHS]

WHITE: You know, it’s a researcher into the states of consciousness and being. Into the alignment between the mind and the body. It’s full of research. Full of personal research. 

LIU: This is why I believe when once upon a time at a leadership offsite you were asked to prompt AI to demonstrate, to build, like, a mascot for you, and I think that mascot was also doing yoga. 

WHITE: It was. I asked my … I asked one of my copilots to generate a picture of me based on everything it knows, and it created a cat doing yoga. 

LIU: [LAUGHS] I love it. OK, so lastly, and this is less “lightning round” and more like “take your time.” What would you like listeners of this podcast to take away from this conversation? You know, about you, about professional life, about research, about making … or maybe even just making choices. 

WHITE: You know, I think it’s about the power of adaptability and the diversity of experience. You know, it’s about being open to what wants to happen, what needs to happen. You know, being open, called to serve, willingness to change. 

LIU: I like that. 

So thank you, Chris—Dr. White—for joining me, and to our audience, thank you for listening. 

WHITE: Thanks, Wei. 

[MUSIC]
